1
夫有國有家者，禮儀之用尚矣。 然而歷代損益，每有不同，非務相改，隨時之宜故也。 漢文以人情季薄，國喪革三年之紀； 光武以中興崇儉，七廟有共堂之制； 魏祖以侈惑宜矯，終歛去襲稱之數； 晉武以丘郊不異，二至并南北之祀。 互相即襲，以訖于今，豈三代之典不存哉，取其應時之變而已。 且閔子譏古禮，退而致事； 叔孫創漢制，化流後昆。 由此言之，任己而不師古，秦氏以之致亡，師古而不適用，王莽所以身滅。 然則漢、魏以來，各揆古今之中，以通一代之儀。 司馬彪集後漢眾注，以為禮儀志，校其行事，已與前漢頗不同矣。 況三國鼎峙，歷晉至宋，時代移改，各隨事立。 自漢末剝亂，舊章乖弛，魏初則王粲、衞覬典定眾儀； 蜀朝則孟光、許慈創理制度； 晉始則荀顗、鄭沖詳定晉禮； 江左則荀崧、刁協緝理乖紊。 其間名儒通學，諸所論敍，往往新出，非可悉載。 今抄魏氏以後經國誕章，以備此志云。
Whether one rules a realm or heads a household, the observance of ritual stands foremost. Yet every dynasty has trimmed or expanded the ritual code in its own way—not from mere innovation, but to suit the needs of the age. Emperor Wen of Han, finding popular sentiment too slack for full mourning, shortened the state's three-year bereavement; Guangwu, reviving the dynasty in frugal spirit, housed the seven temples under one roof; Cao Cao, deeming luxury a corruption to be checked, eventually abolished the series of posthumous epithets; Emperor Wu of Jin, treating the suburban rites as one, merged the northern and southern sacrifices at the solstices. Dynasties have followed one another in this fashion down to our day. The rites of the Three Dynasties are not lost; each age simply takes what fits its moment. Min Ziqian once condemned archaic ritual and retired from office to tend his duties; Shusun Tong devised the Han ceremonial order, and his reforms shaped generations to come. Thus to follow only one's own judgment and spurn antiquity was the Qin's ruin; to cite antiquity yet fail to apply it was Wang Mang's destruction. Since Han and Wei times, each court has weighed past and present to frame its own ritual order. Sima Biao compiled Later Han ritual notes into a treatise; even by his day practice had diverged sharply from Former Han. Still more under the Three Kingdoms, through Jin to Song: as times changed, each regime shaped ritual to its circumstances. When Han collapsed, old rules broke down; early Wei turned to Wang Can and Wei Jian to settle the public rites; Shu had Meng Guang and Xu Ci establish its ritual framework; Early Jin charged Xun Yi and Zheng Chong with codifying its ritual code; South of the Yangzi, Xun Song and Diao Xie sorted out what had fallen into disorder. Learned men in between proposed new schemes at every turn—far too many to record in full. Here I excerpt the founding ritual statutes from Wei onward for this treatise.
2
魏文帝雖受禪于漢，而以夏數為得天，故黃初元年詔曰：「孔子稱『行夏之時，乘殷之輅，服周之冕，樂則韶舞。 』此聖人集羣代之美事，為後王制法也。 傳曰『夏數為得天』。 朕承唐、虞之美，至於正朔，當依虞、夏故事。 若殊徽號，異器械，制禮樂，易服色，用牲幣，自當隨土德之數。 每四時之季月，服黃十八日，臘以丑，牲用白，其飾節旄，自當赤，但節幡黃耳。 其餘郊祀天地朝會四時之服，宜如漢制。 宗廟所服，一如周禮。 」尚書令桓階等奏：「據三正周復之義，國家承漢氏人正之後，當受之以地正，犧牲宜用白，今從漢十三月正，則犧牲不得獨改。 今新建皇統，宜稽古典先代，以從天命，而告朔犧牲，壹皆不改，非所以明革命之義也。 」詔曰：「服色如所奏。 其餘宜如虞承唐，但臘日用丑耳，此亦聖人之制也。」
Though Emperor Wen of Wei took the throne from Han, he held the Xia calendar to possess Heaven's mandate; in Huangchu year one he proclaimed: "Confucius said, 'Adopt Xia's calendar, Yin's carriages, Zhou's caps, and for music the Shao and Wu dances. "'—the sage gathering the finest practices of every age to set law for kings to come. Tradition holds that "the Xia calendar obtained Heaven." I inherit the glory of Tang and Yu; for the civil calendar I shall follow the precedent of Yu and Xia. Changes to titles, regalia, ritual, music, dress, or sacrificial offerings should follow the reckoning of our earthly virtue. In each season's final month yellow dress is worn for eighteen days; the year-end sacrifice falls on a chou day with white victims; banner staffs are red, pennants yellow. All other garb for suburban rites, court assemblies, and the four seasons should follow Han usage. Temple vestments shall follow Zhou ritual in full." Huan Jie and others submitted: "By the doctrine of the three beginnings, a dynasty succeeding Han's human beginning should adopt the earthly beginning and use white victims. Yet if we keep Han's thirteenth-month new year, victims alone cannot change." In founding a new dynasty we should consult antiquity and obey Heaven—yet to leave the calendar announcement and sacrificial victims unchanged fails to proclaim revolution." The edict replied: "Dress and color as you propose. Otherwise follow Yu inheriting Tang, but keep the year-end sacrifice on a chou day—that too is the sage's rule."
3
明帝即位，便有改正朔之意，朝議多異同，故持疑不決。 久乃下詔曰：「黃初以來，諸儒共論正朔，或以改之為宜，或以不改為是，意取駁異，于今未決。 朕在東宮時聞之，意常以為夫子作春秋，通三統，為後王法。 正朔各從色，不同因襲。 自五帝、三王以下，或父子相繼，同體異德； 或納大麓，受終文祖； 或尋干戈，從天行誅。 雖遭遇異時，步驟不同，然未有不改正朔，用服色，表明文物，以章受命之符也。 由此言之，何必以不改為是邪。」
Emperor Ming wished from the first to reform the calendar, but court opinion split and he hesitated. At last he decreed: "Since Huangchu, scholars have disputed the calendar—some urging change, some urging continuity—and the matter remains unsettled. In the Eastern Palace I concluded that Confucius, writing the Spring and Autumn, embraced the three systems to legislate for future kings. Each new beginning has its own color and does not merely inherit the last. Since the Five Emperors and Three Kings, some fathers and sons ruled in succession yet with different virtue; some received the Mandate on the great map and completed Wen's work; some seized power by arms and punished in Heaven's name. Whatever the path to power, none failed to reform the calendar, change dress and color, and display regalia to mark receipt of the Mandate. So why insist that not changing is correct?"
4
於是公卿以下博議。 侍中高堂隆議曰：「按自古有文章以來，帝王之興，受禪之與干戈，皆改正朔，所以明天道，定民心也。 易曰：『革，元亨利貞。 』『有孚改命吉。 』『湯武革命，應乎天，從乎人。 』其義曰，水火更用事，猶王者必改正朔易服色也。 易通卦驗曰：『王者必改正朔，易服色，以應天地三氣三色。 』書曰：『若稽古帝舜曰重華，建皇授政改朔。 』初『高陽氏以十一月為正，薦玉以赤繒。 高辛氏以十三月為正，薦玉以白繒。 』尚書傳曰：『舜定鍾石，論人聲，乃及鳥獸，咸變於前。 故更四時，改堯正。 』詩曰：『一之日觱發，二之日栗烈，三之日于耜。 』傳曰：『一之日，周正月，二之日，殷正月，三之日，夏正月。 』詩推度災曰：『如有繼周而王者，雖百世可知。 以前檢後，文質相因，法度相改。 三而復者，正色也，二而復者，文質也。 』以前檢後，謂軒轅、高辛、夏后氏、漢皆以十三月為正； 少昊、有唐、有殷皆以十二月為正； 高陽、有虞、有周皆以十一月為正。 後雖百世，皆以前代三而復也。 禮大傳曰：『聖人南面而治天下，必正度量，考文章，改正朔，易服色，殊徽號。 』樂稽曜嘉曰：『禹將受位，天意大變，迅風雷雨，以明將去虞而適夏也。 是以舜禹雖繼平受禪，猶制禮樂，改正朔，以應天從民。 夏以十三月為正，法物之始，其色尚黑。 殷以十二月為正，法物之牙，其色尚白。 周以十一月為正，法物之萌，其色尚赤。 能察其類，能正其本，則嶽瀆致雲雨，四時和，五稼成，麟皇翔集。 』春秋：『十七年夏六月甲子朔，日有蝕之。 』傳曰：『當夏四月，是謂孟夏。 』春秋元命苞曰：『王者受命，昭然明於天地之理，故必移居處，更稱號，改正朔，易服色，以明天命聖人之寶，質文再而改，窮則相承，周則復始，正朔改則天命顯。 』凡典籍所記，不盡於此，略舉大較，亦足以明也。」
Thereupon ministers and officials debated at length. Gao Tanglong argued: "In every age, whether a throne was taken by abdication or by war, rulers reformed the calendar to clarify Heaven's way and steady the people. The Changes says: 'Revolution: supreme success, perseverance brings good fortune. ' 'With sincerity, changing the mandate is auspicious. ' 'Tang and Wu made revolution, answering Heaven and following the people. The meaning is that as water and fire alternate in cosmic office, so kings must reform the calendar and change dress and color. The Tong Gua Yan says: 'Kings must reform the calendar and change dress and color to answer Heaven and Earth's three qi and three colors. The Documents say of Shun: 'He received the imperial charge and reformed the calendar. Gaoyang first took the eleventh month as new year and offered jade with red silk. Gaoxin took the thirteenth month as new year and offered jade with white silk. The Documents tradition says Shun tuned bells and stones, and even birds and beasts changed before him. Thus he altered the four seasons and changed Yao's calendar. The Odes say: 'First day—the bitter blast; second day—the piercing cold; third day—the ploughing. The tradition explains: the first day is Zhou's new year, the second Yin's, the third Xia's. The Tui Du Zai says: 'Whoever succeeds Zhou as king—even a hundred generations hence may be known. Looking backward to infer forward, substance and ornament cycle, and institutions shift in turn. What cycles in threes is correct color; what cycles in twos is substance and ornament. By this rule Huangdi, Gaoxin, Xia, and Han all used the thirteenth month as new year; Shaohao, Tang, and Yin used the twelfth month; Gaoyang, Yu, and Zhou used the eleventh month. A hundred generations later, each still turned on the cycle of three. The Ritual Great Tradition says the sage governing south must fix measures, examine texts, reform the calendar, change dress and color, and distinguish titles. The Yue Ji Yao Jia says that when Yu was to receive the throne, Heaven sent wind and thunder to show the shift from Shun to Xia. So though Shun and Yu took the throne peacefully by abdication, they still reformed ritual, music, and calendar to answer Heaven and the people. Xia used the thirteenth month, taking the origin of things as its model; its color was black. Yin used the twelfth month, taking the sprouting of things as its model; its color was white. Zhou used the eleventh month, taking the budding of things as its model; its color was red. When categories are discerned and the root rectified, rain falls, seasons harmonize, grain ripens, and auspicious beasts appear. The Spring and Autumn records: 'Summer, sixth month, jiazi, first of the month—solar eclipse. The tradition says this was Xia's fourth month—the first month of summer. The Yuan Ming Bao says a new king must move his capital, change his title, reform the calendar, and change dress and color so the Mandate shines forth; substance and ornament alternate by twos in endless cycle—reform the calendar and the Mandate appears. The classics say more than this; the outline alone suffices to prove the point."
5
太尉司馬懿、尚書僕射衞臻、尚書薛悌、中書監劉放、中書侍郎刁幹、博士秦靜、趙怡、中候中詔季岐以為宜改； 侍中繆襲、散騎常侍王肅、尚書郎魏衡、太子舍人黃史嗣以為不宜改。
Sima Yi, Wei Zhen, Xue Ti, Liu Fang, Diao Gan, Qin Jing, Zhao Yi, and Li Qi favored reform; Miao Xi, Wang Su, Wei Heng, and Huang Shisi opposed it.
6
青龍五年，山茌縣言黃龍見。 帝乃詔三公曰：
In Qinglong year five, Shanzhi county reported a yellow dragon. The emperor then addressed the Three Excellencies:
7
:昔在庖犧，繼天而王，始據木德，為羣代首。 自茲以降，服物氏號，開元著統者，既膺受命曆數之期，握皇靈遷興之運，承天改物，序其綱紀。 雖炎、黃、少昊，顓頊、高辛，唐、虞、夏后，世系相襲，同氣共祖，猶豫昭顯所受之運，著明天人去就之符，無不革易制度，更定禮樂，延羣后，班瑞信，使之煥炳可述于後也。 至于正朔之事，當明示變改，以彰異代，曷疑其不然哉。
In the age of Fuxi, first to succeed Heaven as king, he took wood as his virtue and led all generations. Thereafter every founder who received the Mandate and opened a reign, grasping Heaven's favor, received its charge, changed institutions, and set his dynasty in order. Even when rulers shared one lineage—from the Yellow Emperor through Yu and Xia—they still proclaimed the fortune they received, showed Heaven's sign, reformed institutions, reset ritual and music, summoned the feudal lords, and distributed the credence tally, leaving a brilliant record for posterity. On the calendar itself, the change should be made plain to mark a new age—how can there be doubt?
8
:文皇帝踐阼之初，庶事草創，遂襲漢正，不革其統。 朕在東宮，及臻在位，每覽書籍之林，總公卿之議。 夫言三統相變者，有明文； 云虞、夏相因者，無其言也。 曆志曰：「天統之正在子，物萌而赤； 地統之正在丑，物化而白； 人統之正在寅，物成而黑。 」但含生氣，以微成著。 故太極運三辰五星於上，元氣轉三統五行於下，登降周旋，終則又始，言天地與人所以相通也。 仲尼以大聖之才，祖述堯、舜，範章文、武，制作春秋，論究人事，以貫百王之則。 故於三微之月，每月稱王，以明三正迭相為首。 夫祖述堯、舜，以論三正，則其明義，豈使近在殷、周而已乎。 朕以眇身，繼承洪緒，既不能紹上聖之遺風，揚先帝之休德，又使王教之弛者不張，帝典之闕者未補，亹亹之德不著，亦惡可已乎。
When Emperor Wen first took the throne, affairs were still being founded, so he kept Han's calendar unchanged. In the Eastern Palace and on the throne I have read widely and weighed the ministers' debates. That the three systems rotate is plainly written; but that Yu and Xia simply continued one another is nowhere said. The Calendar Treatise says: "Heaven's system begins at zi, when things bud and are red; Earth's system begins at chou, when things transform and are white; Man's system begins at yin, when things mature and are black." Life-breath grows from the minute to the manifest. The Supreme Ultimate moves sun, moon, and stars above; primordial qi turns the three systems and five phases below—rising and falling in cycle without end, Heaven, Earth, and man in communion. Confucius, greatest of sages, followed Yao and Shun, modeled Wen and Wu, wrote the Spring and Autumn, and weighed human affairs to bind the rule of a hundred kings. In the months of the three micro-beginnings he named a king for each month, showing how the three calendars rotate as chief. In following Yao and Shun to expound the three beginnings, how could the meaning be confined to Yin and Zhou alone? I, slight as I am, have inherited a great mandate; I have neither revived the supreme sages' legacy nor enlarged my father's virtue, and royal teaching lies slack and imperial canon unfinished—how can I do nothing?
9
:今推三統之次，魏得地統，當以建丑之月為正。 考之羣藝，厥義彰矣。 改青龍五年春三月為景初元年孟夏四月。 服色尚黃，犧牲用白，戎事乘黑首之白馬，建大赤之旗，朝會建大白之旗。 春夏秋冬孟仲季月，雖與正歲不同，至於郊祀迎氣，礿、祀、烝、嘗，巡狩、蒐田，分至啟閉，班宣時令，中氣晚早，敬授民事，諸若此者，皆以正歲斗建為節。 此曆數之序，乃上與先聖合符同契，重規疊矩者也。 今遵其義，庶可以顯祖考大造之基，崇有魏維新之命。
Now, by the order of the three systems, Wei has the earthly system and should take the month of establishment at chou as new year. Examined against the classics, the meaning is clear. The third month of spring, Qinglong year five, becomes the first month of summer, Jingchu year one. Dress and color are yellow; victims white; in war ride white horses with black heads; raise the great red banner in the field and the great white at court. Though seasonal months now differ from the civil year, suburban rites, qi observances, seasonal sacrifices, hunts, solstices, and agricultural commands still follow the Dipper's position in the civil year. This calendrical order matches the former sages, rule upon rule. By following it we display our ancestors' great foundation and exalt Great Wei's mandate of renewal.
10
:於戲！ 王公羣后，百辟卿士，靖康厥職，帥意無怠，以永天休。 司徒露布，咸使聞知，稱朕意焉。
Alas! Princes, lords, and ministers—fulfill your offices faithfully, lead without slackening, and so win Heaven's lasting grace. Let the Minister of Education issue a public notice so all may hear it and know my will.
11
案服色尚黃，據土行也。 犧牲旂旗，一用殷禮，行殷之時故也。 周禮巾車職，「建大赤以朝」，「大白以即戎」，此則周以正色之旗朝，以先代之旗即戎。 魏用殷禮，變周之制，故建大白朝，大赤即戎也。 明帝又詔曰：「以建寅之月為正者，其牲用玄； 以建丑之月為正者，其牲用白； 以建子之月為正者，其牲用騂。 此為牲色各從其正，不隨所祀之陰陽也。 祭天不嫌於用玄，則祭地不得獨疑於用白也。 天地用牲，得無不宜異邪？ 更議。 」於是議者各有引據，無適可從。 又詔曰：「諸議所依據各參錯，若陽祀用騂，陰祀用黝，復云祭天用玄，祭地用黃，如此，用牲之義，未為通也。 天地至尊，用牲當同以所尚之色，不得專以陰陽為別也。 今祭皇皇帝天、皇皇后地、天地郊、明堂、宗廟，皆宜用白。 其別祭五郊，各隨方色，祭日月星辰之類用騂，社稷山川之屬用玄，此則尊卑方色，陰陽眾義暢矣。」
Dress and color honor yellow because Wei rests on the Earth phase. Victims, banners, and flags all follow Yin ritual, since Wei adopts Yin's calendrical phase. The Rites of Zhou's Office of Bannered Chariots says to raise the great red banner at court and the great white for war—Zhou thus flew its own color in peace and an earlier dynasty's color in war. Wei adopted Yin ritual and altered Zhou's practice, so it raised the great white at court and the great red in war. Emperor Ming further decreed: "Where the year begins at the month of establishment at yin, victims should be black; Where it begins at the month of establishment at chou, victims should be white; Where it begins at the month of establishment at zi, victims should be red bulls. Thus each calendar's victim color follows its own new year, not the yin or yang of the rite being performed. If Heaven sacrifice may use black victims without objection, Earth sacrifice cannot be singled out for questioning the use of white. Should the victims for Heaven and Earth not be the same? Reconsider the matter. Each debater cited different authorities, and no single view could be adopted. He decreed again: "Your arguments contradict one another: yang rites use red bulls and yin rites dark victims, yet some say Heaven takes black and Earth yellow—under such rules the meaning of victim choice is incoherent. Heaven and Earth are supreme; their victims should share the same honored color and must not be split by yin-yang categories alone. Henceforth white victims should be used for Imperial August Heaven, Imperial August Earth, the joint suburban rites, the Bright Hall, and the ancestral temples. At the five directional suburbs each color follows its quarter; sun, moon, and stars take red bulls, while soil-and-grain altars and mountains and rivers take black victims—so rank, direction, yin, yang, and every other principle are harmonized."
12
三年正月，帝崩，齊王即位。 是年十二月，尚書盧毓奏：「烈祖明皇帝以今年正日棄離萬國，禮，忌日不樂，甲乙之謂也。 烈祖明皇帝建丑之月棄天下，臣妾之情，於此正日，有甚甲乙。 今若以建丑正朝四方，會羣臣，設盛樂，不合於禮。 」博士樂祥議：「正日旦受朝貢，羣臣奉贄； 後五日，乃大宴會作樂。 」太尉屬朱誕議：「今因宜改之際，還修舊則，元首建寅，於制為便。 」大將軍屬劉肇議：「宜過正一日乃朝賀大會，明令天下，知崩亡之日不朝也。 」詔曰：「省奏事，五內斷絕，奈何奈何！ 烈祖明皇帝以正日棄天下，每與皇太后念此日至，心有剝裂。 不可以此日朝羣辟，受慶賀也。 月二日會，又非故也。 聽當還夏正月。 雖違先帝通三統之義，斯亦子孫哀慘永懷。 又夏正朔得天數者，其以建寅之月為歲首。」
In the first month of the third year the emperor died, and the Prince of Qi succeeded him. That December, Minister Lu Yu of the Masters of Writing memorialized: "Our late Emperor Ming left the realm on this year's New Year's Day; ritual forbids music on a day of mourning—this is the rule of jia and yi. Emperor Ming died in the month of establishment at chou; for subjects and consorts, grief on this New Year's Day weighs far more than any jia or yi taboo. To hold New Year's court for the four quarters, gather the ministers, and stage grand music in the month of establishment at chou would violate ritual. Academician Yue Xiang argued: "On New Year's Day at dawn receive tribute at court and let the ministers present their gifts; then five days later hold the great feast with music." Attendant Zhu Dan of the Grand Commandant argued: "Now, when change is timely, restore the old rule: let the sovereign's year begin at the month of establishment at yin, which suits the institutions." Attendant Liu Zhao of the General-in-Chief argued: "Court congratulations should wait until the day after New Year's Day, so the realm knows that the day of death is not a day of audience." The decree read: "Reading your memorials tears my heart apart—what can be done, what can be done! Our late Emperor Ming died on New Year's Day; whenever the Empress Dowager and I mark that day, our hearts are torn. We cannot hold court for the ministers or accept congratulations on that day. A gathering on the second of the month is not the old custom either. You are permitted to return to the Xia first month. Though this departs from the late emperor's doctrine of the three rotating systems, it expresses the descendants' lasting grief. Moreover, the Xia new year matches Heaven's reckoning; let the month of establishment at yin be the year's beginning."
13
晉武帝泰始二年九月，羣公奏：「唐堯、舜、禹不以易祚改制； 至於湯、武，各推行數。 宣尼答為邦之問，則曰行夏之時，輅冕之制，通為百代之言。 蓋期於從政濟治，不繫於行運也。 今大晉繼三皇之蹤，踵舜、禹之迹，應天從民，受禪有魏，宜一用前代正朔服色，皆如有虞遵唐故事，於義為弘。 」奏可。 孫盛曰：「仍舊，非也。 且晉為金行，服色尚赤，考之天道，其違甚矣。 」及宋受禪，亦如魏、晉故事。
In the ninth month of Taishi year two, the assembled lords memorialized to Emperor Wu of Jin: "Yao, Shun, and Yu did not change institutions when they changed rulers; only Tang and Wu each advanced the calendrical phase. When Confucius was asked how to govern a state, he said to follow Xia's calendar and Zhou's carriage and regalia—counsel honored for a hundred generations. The point was effective government, not loyalty to a dynastic phase. Great Jin now follows the Three Sovereigns and treads in the steps of Shun and Yu, answering Heaven and the people and receiving Wei's abdication; it should keep the former calendar and regalia, as Yu followed Yao's example—a generous course in principle. The memorial was approved. Sun Sheng wrote: "To keep the old ways was wrong. Jin belonged to the Metal phase and should have honored red; measured against Heaven's Way, the breach was grave. When Song received the abdication, it too followed the Wei and Jin precedent.
14
魏明帝初，司空王朗議：「古者有年數，無年號，漢初猶然。 或有世而改，有中元、後元。 元改彌數，中、後之號不足，故更假取美名，非古也。 述春秋之事，曰隱公元年，則簡而易知。 載漢世之事，曰建元元年，則後不見。 宜若古稱元而已。 」明帝不從。 乃詔曰：「先帝即位之元，則有延康之號，受禪之初，亦有黃初之稱。 今名年可也。 」於是尚書奏：「易曰：『乾道變化，各正性命。 保合大和，乃利貞。 首出庶物，萬國咸寧。 』宜為太和元年。 」詔 〈闕〉
Early in Emperor Ming of Wei's reign, Minister of Works Wang Lang argued: "Antiquity counted years but had no era names, as early Han still did. Sometimes a new reign brought Zhongyuan or Houyuan. Yuan reigns multiplied until Zhong and Hou no longer sufficed, so ever finer names were invented—this is not ancient practice. To tell Spring and Autumn events as "the first year of Duke Yin" is concise and clear. To record Han events as "the first year of Jianyuan" leaves what follows obscure. One should name the year Yuan alone, as antiquity did. Emperor Ming did not agree. He decreed: "When the late emperor first took the throne there was Yankang; at the abdication there was Huangchu. Naming the year is acceptable now. The Masters of Writing then memorialized: "The Changes says: 'The Way of Qian transforms and changes, giving each thing its proper nature and fate. Preserving and harmonizing the great harmony brings benefit and steadfastness. Leading forth the myriad things, it brings peace to every state. ' The era should be called Taihe, year one. The decree 〈Missing text in source.〉

周之五禮，其五為嘉。 嘉□□春秋左氏傳曰：「晉侯問襄公年，季武子對曰：『會于沙隨之歲，寡君以生。 』晉侯曰：『十二年矣，是謂一終。 一星終也。 國君十五而生子。 冠而生子，禮也。 君可以冠矣。 大夫盍為冠具。 』武子對曰：『君冠必以祼享之禮行之，以金石之樂節之，以先君之祧處之。 今君在行，未可具也。 請及兄弟之國而假備焉。 』晉侯許諾。 還及衞，冠于成公之廟，假鍾磬焉，禮也。 」賈、服說皆以為人君禮十二而冠也。 古尚書說武王崩，成王年十三。 推武王以庚辰歲崩，周公以壬午歲出居東，以癸未歲反。 禮周公冠成王，命史祝辭。 辭，告也。 是除喪冠也。 周公居東未反，成王冠弁以開金縢之書，時十六矣。 是成王年十五服除，周公冠之而後出也。 按禮、傳之文，則天子諸侯近十二，遠十五，必冠矣。 周禮雖有服冕之數，而無天子冠文。 儀禮云：「公侯之有冠禮，夏之末造。 」王、鄭皆以為夏末上下相亂，篡弒由生，故作公侯冠禮，則明無天子冠禮之審也。 大夫又無冠禮。 古者五十而後爵，何大夫冠禮之有？ 周人年五十而有賢才，則試以大夫之事，猶行士禮也。 故筮日筮賓，冠於阼以著代，醮於客位，三加彌尊。 皆士禮耳。 然漢氏以來，天子諸侯，頗采其議。 志曰「儀從冠禮」是也。 漢順帝冠，又兼用曹襃新禮。 襃新禮今不存。 禮儀志又云：「乘輿初加緇布進賢，次爵弁、武弁，次通天，皆於高廟。 王公以下，初加進賢而已。 」按此文始冠緇布，從古制也，冠於宗廟是也。 魏天子冠一加，其說曰，士禮三加，加有成也。 至於天子諸侯，無加數之文者，將以踐阼臨民，尊極德備，豈得復與士同？ 此言非也。 夫以聖人之才，猶三十而立，況十二之年，未及志學，便謂德成，無所勸勉，非理實也。 魏氏太子再加，皇子、王公世子乃三加。 孫毓以為一加再加皆非也。 禮醮詞曰「令月吉日」，又「以歲之正，以月之令」。 魯襄公冠以冬，漢惠帝冠以三月，明無定月也。 後漢以來，帝加元服，咸以正月。 晉咸寧二年秋閏九月，遣使冠汝南王柬，此則晉禮亦有非必歲首也。 禮冠於廟，魏以來不復在廟。 然晉武、惠冠太子，皆即廟見，斯亦擬在廟之儀也。 晉穆帝、孝武將冠，先以幣告廟，訖又廟見也。
Of the Zhou five rituals, the fifth is the festive rite. On the festive rite—two characters are lost in the transmitted text—the Zuo Commentary says: "The Marquis of Jin asked Duke Xiang's age. Ji Wuzi answered: 'In the year of the meeting at Shasui, our lord was born." '" The Marquis said: "Twelve years—that is one full cycle. One stellar cycle has run its course. A ruler should beget a son by fifteen. To come of age and then beget a son is proper ritual. Your lord may now receive the cap. Ministers ought to prepare the capping gear. '" Wuzi replied: "A lord's capping must follow the libation sacrifice, be paced by bells and stones, and be held at the shrine of his ancestor. Our lord is traveling and the rite cannot yet be readied. I ask to borrow what is needed from a friendly state and perform it there. '" The Marquis of Jin consented. On the return through Wei he was capped in Duke Cheng's temple, borrowing bells and chime-stones—proper ritual. Jia and Fu both held that a ruler should be capped at twelve. The old Documents tradition says King Cheng was thirteen when King Wu died. Reckoning backward: King Wu died in gengchen; the Duke of Zhou went east in renwu and returned in guiwei. By ritual the Duke of Zhou capped King Cheng and had the recorder pronounce the invocation. "Ci" means to declare. This was the capping that followed the end of mourning. Before the Duke of Zhou returned from the east, King Cheng put on his bian cap to open the metal-bound casket—he was then sixteen. So when King Cheng was fifteen and mourning ended, the Duke of Zhou capped him before going east. By ritual and commentary, Son of Heaven and feudal lords must be capped—at earliest twelve, at latest fifteen. The Rites of Zhou lists court robes and caps but says nothing of the Son of Heaven's capping. The Ceremonial says: "The capping of lords and marquises dates from late Xia. Wang and Zheng held that late Xia fell into disorder and usurpation, so a capping rite was made for lords and marquises—clear proof that no Son of Heaven's capping rite existed. Great officers had no capping rite either. In antiquity rank came only after fifty—what capping rite could a great officer have? Among the Zhou, a man of talent at fifty might be tried in a great officer's duties, yet still underwent the common officer's rite. Hence one divines day and guest, caps at the eastern steps to mark succession, offers libation at the guest seat, and with three additions grows ever more honored. All of this is common-officer ritual. Yet since Han, Son of Heaven and feudal lords have largely followed these views. The Treatise's phrase "ceremony follows the capping rite" refers to this. At Emperor Shun of Han's capping, Cao Bao's new rite was used as well. Cao Bao's new rite no longer survives. The Treatise on Ritual and Ceremony also says: "The emperor first receives the black-cloth advance-the-worthy cap, then the noble cap and martial cap, then the all-penetrating cap—all at the High Temple. For kings, dukes, and those below, only the first advance-the-worthy cap is added. This text shows the first cap was black cloth, following ancient custom, and capping at the ancestral temple was correct. Under Wei the Son of Heaven received only one cap; the explanation was that in common-officer ritual three additions mark full maturity. For Son of Heaven and feudal lords, lacking any text on how many caps to add, some argued that ascending the throne and ruling the people made honor and virtue complete—so how could they share the common officer's rite? That argument is wrong. Even a sage is only "established at thirty"; at twelve, before the age of eager study, to declare virtue complete and offer no further encouragement is unreasonable. Under Wei the heir apparent received two caps; imperial princes and heir sons of kings and dukes received three. Sun Yu held that whether one cap was added or several, both approaches were wrong. The ritual invocation reads, "On this fortunate month and day," and again, "With the year's right season, with the month's proper order." Duke Xiang of Lu received the cap in winter, and Emperor Hui of Han in the third month—clear proof that no single month was prescribed. From Later Han onward, every emperor's coming-of-age capping took place in the first month. In Jin's second year of Xianning, during the intercalary ninth month of autumn, an envoy capped the Prince of Runan, Sima Jian—showing that Jin ritual as well need not fall at the New Year. Ritual prescribed capping in the ancestral temple, but from Wei onward the ceremony was no longer held there. Yet when Emperors Wu and Hui capped the crown prince, each then appeared before the temple—a practice that still echoed the temple-based rite. Before Emperors Mu and Xiaowu were capped, they first announced the event to the temple with silk offerings, and afterward appeared there again when the rite was complete.
16
晉惠帝之為太子將冠也，武帝臨軒，使兼司徒高陽王珪加冠，兼光祿勳、屯騎校尉華廙贊冠。 江左諸帝將冠，金石宿設，百僚陪位。 又豫於殿上鋪大牀。 御府令奉冕幘簪導袞服，以授侍中、常侍。 太尉加幘，太保加冕。 將加冕，太尉跪讀祝文曰：「令月吉日，始加元服。 皇帝穆穆，思弘袞職。 欽若昊天，六合是式。 率遵祖考，永永無極。 眉壽惟期，介茲景福。 」加冕訖，侍中繫玄紞。 侍中脫絳紗服，加袞服。 冠事畢，太保率羣臣奉觴上壽，王公以下三稱萬歲，乃退。 按儀注，一加幘冕而已。
When the crown prince who would become Emperor Hui was to be capped, Emperor Wu presided from the throne hall and appointed Prince Gui of Gaoyang, serving concurrently as Minister of Education, to place the cap, with Hua Yong, concurrently Director of the Imperial Household and Colonel of the Colony Cavalry, to assist. Before an emperor south of the Yangzi was capped, bells and stone chimes were set out the night before, and the full corps of officials took their places beside him. A large couch was also laid out in advance on the hall floor. The Superintendent of the Imperial Wardrobe brought forward the cap, headcloth, hairpin, cap guide, and dragon robe and handed them to the Attendant Within and the Regular Attendant. The Grand Commandant placed the headcloth; the Grand Guardian placed the cap. As the cap was about to be set on his head, the Grand Commandant knelt and read the invocation: "On this fortunate month and day, you now first receive the cap of full manhood. Solemn is the emperor, mindful to fulfill the great office of the dragon robe. In reverent accord with vast Heaven, may the six directions be your measure. Following the path of ancestors and forefathers, without end through endless time. May long life be your portion; may this resplendent blessing be conferred upon you. " When the cap had been placed, the Attendant Within fastened the black headband. The Attendant Within removed the crimson gauze garment and put on the dragon robe. When the capping was finished, the Grand Guardian led the officials in raising cups to wish long life; princes, dukes, and all ranks below called "Ten thousand years!" three times, and then withdrew. According to the written protocols, only one headcloth and one cap were added.

宋冠皇太子及蕃王，亦一加也。 官有其注。 晉武帝泰始十年，南宮王承年十五，依舊應冠。 有司議奏：「禮十五成童。 國君十五而生子，以明可冠之宜。 又漢、魏遣使冠諸王，非古典。 」於是制諸王十五冠，不復加命。 元嘉十一年，營道侯將冠。 詔曰：「營道侯義綦可克日冠。 外詳舊施行。 」何楨冠儀約制及王堪私撰冠儀，亦皆家人之可遵用者也。
Under the Song dynasty as well, the crown prince and territorial princes received only a single cap in the ceremony. The relevant offices kept written regulations to that effect. In the tenth year of Taishi under Emperor Wu of Jin, the Prince of Nangong, Cheng, turned fifteen and by established rule was due to be capped. The responsible offices debated the matter and memorialized: "By ritual, fifteen marks the age of a mature youth. A state's ruler fathers a son at fifteen, which shows when capping is proper. Moreover, Han and Wei's practice of sending envoys to cap the feudal princes was not ancient ritual. " Thereupon a rule was issued that all princes be capped at fifteen, without waiting for a separate imperial appointment. In the eleventh year of Yuanjia, the Marquis of Yingdao was approaching his capping ceremony. An edict proclaimed: "The Marquis of Yingdao, Yiqi, may fix a day for his capping. Let the external offices arrange the ceremony according to former practice. He Zhen's summarized capping protocols and Wang Kan's privately drafted capping manual were likewise household guides that families could follow.

魏齊王正始四年，立皇后甄氏，其儀不存。
In the fourth year of Zhengshi under the Qi emperor of Wei, Empress Zhen was installed, but the ceremony itself has not survived.

晉武帝咸寧二年，臨軒，遣太尉賈充策立后楊氏，納悼后也。 因大赦，賜王公以下各有差。 百僚上禮。
In the second year of Xianning, Emperor Wu of Jin presided at the throne hall and sent Grand Commandant Jia Chong with a written appointment to establish Empress Yang—thus he took Empress Daohou as his consort. A general amnesty followed, and princes, dukes, and all ranks below received gifts graded by station. The full body of officials presented congratulatory offerings.

太康八年，有司奏：「昏禮納徵，大昏用玄纁，束帛加珪，馬二駟； 王侯玄纁，束帛加璧，乘馬； 大夫用玄纁，束帛加羊。 古者以皮馬為庭實，天子加穀珪，諸侯加大璋。 可依周禮改璧用璋，其羊、雁、酒、米、玄纁如故。 諸侯昏禮加納采告期親迎各帛五匹，及納徵馬四匹，皆令夫家自備，唯璋官為具致之。 」尚書朱整議：「按魏氏故事，王娶妃、公主嫁之禮，天子諸侯以皮馬為庭實，天子加以穀珪，諸侯加以大璋。 漢高后制，聘后黃金二百斤，馬十二匹； 夫人金五十斤，馬四匹。 魏聘后、王娶妃、公主嫁之禮，用絹百九十匹。 晉興，故事用絹三百匹。 」詔曰：「公主嫁由夫氏，不宜皆為備物，賜錢使足而已。 唯給璋，餘如故事。」
In the eighth year of Taikang, the responsible offices memorialized: "For the betrothal gifts in the marriage rite, a great marriage requires dark and red silk, bundled silk with a jade tablet, and two teams of four horses; For kings and marquises, dark and red silk, bundled silk with a jade disk, and riding horses; Great officers should use dark and red silk, bundled silk with a sheep. In antiquity hides and horses served as the court offerings; the Son of Heaven added a grain-pattern jade tablet, and feudal lords added a great jade scepter. Following the Rites of Zhou, the jade disk may be replaced with a scepter; sheep, geese, wine, rice, and dark and red silk should remain unchanged. For a feudal lord's marriage, five bolts of silk should be added for each of the proposing gifts, the announcement of the wedding date, and the groom's arrival, and four horses for the betrothal gift—all to be supplied by the groom's family, except the scepter, which the office should prepare and furnish. " Director of the Masters of Writing Zhu Zheng argued: "By Wei precedent, when a prince took a consort or a princess was given in marriage, the Son of Heaven and feudal lords used hides and horses as court gifts; the Son of Heaven added a grain-pattern jade tablet, and feudal lords a great jade scepter. Under Empress Dowager Gao of Han, betrothal to an empress required two hundred jin of yellow gold and twelve horses; for a consort of lower rank, fifty jin of gold and four horses. Under Wei, betrothal to an empress, a prince's marriage, and a princess's wedding each required one hundred ninety bolts of silk. When Jin came to power, precedent called for three hundred bolts of silk. " An edict replied: "When a princess marries, her husband's family bears the burden; it is not right to supply every item in full—grant money enough to cover the cost and no more. Provide only the scepter; let everything else follow established precedent."
21
成帝咸康二年，臨軒，遣使兼太保領軍將軍諸葛恢、兼太尉護軍將軍孔愉六禮備物，拜皇后杜氏。 即日入宮。 帝御太極殿，羣臣畢賀，非禮也。 王者昏禮，禮無其制。 春秋祭公逆王后于紀。 穀梁、左氏說與公羊又不同。 而漢、魏遺事闕略者眾。 晉武、惠納后，江左又無復儀注，故成帝將納杜后，太常華恒始與博士參定其儀。 據杜預左氏傳說主婚，是供其婚禮之幣而已。 又周靈王求婚於齊，齊侯問於晏桓子，桓子對曰：「夫婦所生若而人，姑姊妹則稱先守某公之遺女若而人。 」此則天子之命，自得下達，臣下之答，徑自上通。 先儒以為丘明詳錄其事，蓋為王者婚娶之禮也。 故成帝臨軒遣使稱制拜后。 然其儀注，又不具存。
In the second year of Xiankang, Emperor Cheng presided at the throne hall and sent Zhuge Hui, concurrently Grand Guardian and General Who Leads the Army, and Kong Yu, concurrently Grand Commandant and General Who Protects the Army, with the full complement of the six marriage gifts to invest Empress Du. She entered the palace that same day. The emperor then took his seat in the Hall of Supreme Ultimate, and the whole court congratulated him—conduct contrary to ritual. The marriage rite for a king appears nowhere in the canonical ritual texts. The Spring and Autumn Annals records that Duke Ji met his queen at Ji. The Guliang and Zuoshi commentaries again disagree with the Gongyang tradition. Yet many Han and Wei precedents survive only in fragments or not at all. After Emperors Wu and Hui took their empresses, the court south of the Yangzi had no surviving ritual manuals, so when Emperor Cheng was to take Empress Du, Minister of Ceremonies Hua Heng first worked with the erudites to fix the ceremony. He relied on Du Yu's reading in the Zuoshi Commentary that the host of the marriage need only furnish the betrothal offerings. Again, when King Ling of Zhou sought a bride from Qi, the Marquis of Qi consulted Yan Huanzi, who answered: "Of the children born to husband and wife, so many; for paternal aunts and sisters, one says, 'The surviving daughters left by the late Lord Such-and-Such, so many.' " This shows that the Son of Heaven's command could pass straight down, and a minister's reply could pass straight up. Earlier scholars thought Zuo Qiuming set the matter down in detail because it illustrated a king's marriage rite. Accordingly, Emperor Cheng presided at the throne hall and sent envoys with an imperial proclamation to invest the empress. Yet even those ritual protocols were not fully preserved.
22
康帝建元元年，納后褚氏。 而儀注陛者不設旄頭。 殿中御史奏：「今迎皇后，依昔成恭皇后入宮御物，而儀注至尊袞冕升殿，旄頭不設，求量處。 又案昔迎恭皇后，唯作青龍旂，其餘皆即御物。 今當臨軒遣使，而立五牛旂旗，旄頭畢罕並出。 即用舊制，今闕。 」詔曰：「所以正法服升太極者，以敬其始，故備其禮也。 今云何更闕所重而撤法物邪？ 又恭后神主入廟，先帝詔后禮宜有降，不宜建五牛旗，而今猶復設之邪！ 既不設五牛旗，則旄頭畢罕之器易具也。 」又詔曰：「舊制既難準，且於今而備，亦非宜。 府庫之儲，唯當以供軍國之費耳。 法服儀飾粗令舉，其餘兼副雜器，停之。」
In the first year of Jianyuan under Emperor Kang, Empress Chu was brought into the palace. Yet the written protocols called for no maotou figures to be posted on the steps. The Palace Censor memorialized: "In receiving the empress now, we should follow Empress Cheng Gong's entry with the imperial regalia at hand; yet the protocols have the sovereign ascending in full dragon robe and cap while no maotou are posted on the steps. We ask how this is to be handled. Moreover, when Empress Gong was received in the past, only the Azure Dragon banner was newly made; everything else was drawn from items already kept in the palace. Now we are to preside at the throne hall and dispatch envoys, yet also erect the Five Ox banners and bring out the maotou and bihan as well. If we are to follow the old system at once, the needed implements are now lacking. " An edict replied: "The sovereign ascends the Hall of Supreme Ultimate in full ceremonial dress to show reverence at the beginning of the rite, and therefore every proper emblem should be in place. Why now omit what matters most and strip away the ritual objects prescribed by law? Again, when Empress Gong's spirit tablet was installed in the temple, the late emperor decreed that an empress's rites should be reduced and the Five Ox banner should not be raised—yet now it is to be raised again! If the Five Ox banner is not erected, the maotou and bihan can easily be supplied. " A further edict said: "Since the old system cannot be followed exactly, and assembling it all at once would be improper even now, the treasury's stores should be reserved only for military and state needs. Provide ceremonial dress and ornaments in rough form, and suspend the rest of the duplicate and miscellaneous implements."
23
及至穆帝升平元年，將納皇后何氏，太常王彪之始更大引經傳及諸故事，以正其禮，深非公羊婚禮不稱主人之義。 又曰：「王者之於四海，無非臣妾。 雖復父兄之親，師友之賢，皆純臣也。 夫崇三綱之始，以定乾坤之儀，安有天父之尊，而稱臣下之命，以納伉儷； 安有臣下之卑，而稱天父之名，以行大禮。 遠尋古禮，無王者此制； 近求史籍，無王者此比。 於情不安，於義不通。 案咸寧二年，納悼皇后時，弘訓太后母臨天下，而無命戚屬之臣為武皇父兄主婚之文。 又考大晉已行之事，咸寧故事，不稱父兄師友，則咸康華恒所上合於舊也。 臣愚謂今納后儀制，宜一依咸康故事。 」於是從之。 華恒所定六禮，云宜依漢舊及大晉已行之制，此恒猶識前事，故王彪之多從咸康，由此也。 惟以取婦之家，三日不舉樂，而咸康羣臣賀為失禮； 故但依咸寧上禮，不復賀也。 其告廟六禮版文等儀，皆彪之所定也。 詳推有典制，其納采版文璽書曰：「皇帝咨前太尉參軍何琦，渾元資始，肇經人倫，爰及夫婦，以奉天地宗廟社稷，謀于公卿，咸以為宜率由舊典。 今使使持節太常彪之、宗正綜以禮納采。 」主人曰：「皇帝嘉命，訪婚陋族，備數采擇。 臣從祖弟故散騎侍郎準之遺女，未閑教訓，衣履若而人，欽承舊章，肅奉典制。 前太尉參軍都鄉侯糞土臣何琦稽首再拜承制詔。 」次問名版文曰：「皇帝曰，咨某官某姓，兩儀配合，承天統物，正位于內，必俟令族，重章舊典。 今使使持節太常某、宗正某，以禮問名。 」主人曰：「皇帝嘉命，使者某到，重宣中詔，問臣名族。 臣族女父母所生先臣故光祿大夫雩婁侯楨之遺玄孫，先臣故豫州刺史關中侯惲之曾孫，先臣故安豐太守關中侯叡之孫，先臣故散騎侍郎準之遺女。 外出自先臣故尚書左丞冑之外曾孫，先臣故侍中關內侯夷之外孫女。 年十七。 欽承舊章，肅奉典制。 」次納吉版文曰：「皇帝曰，咨某官某姓，人謀龜從，僉曰貞吉，敬從典禮。 今使持節太常某、宗正某，以禮納吉。 」主人曰：「皇帝嘉命，使者某重宣中詔，太卜元吉。 臣陋族卑鄙，憂懼不堪。 欽承舊章，肅奉典制。 」次納徵版文：「皇帝曰，咨某官某姓之女，有母儀之德，窈窕之姿，如山如河，宜奉宗廟，永承天祚。 以玄纁皮帛馬羊錢璧，以章典禮。 今使使持節司徒某、太常某，以禮納徵。 」主人曰：「皇帝嘉命，降婚卑陋，崇以上公，寵以典禮，備物典策。 欽承舊章，肅奉典制。 」次請期版文：「皇帝曰，咨某官某姓，謀于公卿，大筮元龜，罔有不臧，率遵典禮。 今使使持節太常某、宗正某，以禮請期。 」主人曰：「皇帝嘉命，使某重宣中詔，吉日惟某可迎。 臣欽承舊章，肅奉典制。 」次親迎版文：「皇帝曰，咨某官某姓，歲吉月令，吉日惟某，率禮以迎。 今使使持節太保某、太尉某以迎。 」主人曰：「皇帝嘉命，使者某重宣中詔。 令月吉辰，備禮以迎。 上公宗卿，兼至副介，近臣百兩。 臣蝝蟻之族，猥承大禮，憂懼戰悸，欽承舊章，肅奉典制。 」其稽首承詔皆如初答。
By the first year of Shengping under Emperor Mu, when Empress He was to be taken, Minister of Ceremonies Wang Biaozhi drew more widely on the classics, commentaries, and precedents to set the rite right, in sharp opposition to the Gongyang view that a royal marriage should not name a host. He argued further: "Toward all within the four seas, the king has no one who is not subject or consort. Even a father or elder brother by blood, or a teacher or friend of virtue, are wholly his subjects. In upholding the Three Bonds that establish the order of Heaven and Earth, how can one who bears Heaven's dignity speak as though a subject's command were needed to take a spouse? And how can a subject, low in station, speak in the name of Heaven's father to conduct the great rite? Searching the distant past in the ritual canon, no king had such a rule; consulting recent historical records, no king had such a precedent. It is emotionally troubling and logically untenable. Consider the second year of Xianning, when Empress Daohou was taken: though the Dowager Empress of Hongxun, as mother, ruled the realm, no document appointed a kinsman or minister to serve as marriage host on behalf of Emperor Wu's father or elder brother. Review what Great Jin had already done: the Xianning precedent named no father, elder brother, teacher, or friend—so Hua Heng's Xiankang proposal accorded with established practice. Your servant humbly submits that the present empress-taking ceremony should follow the Xiankang precedent in full. " The court accepted his recommendation. In fixing the six marriage gifts, Hua Heng had urged adherence to Han custom and to what Great Jin had already done; because Heng still remembered earlier practice, Wang Biaozhi chiefly followed the Xiankang model for that reason. Only on one point did he dissent: the bride's household should keep silence and refrain from music for three days, whereas the ministers' congratulations at Xiankang had been a breach of ritual; so he kept only the Xianning gift presentation and omitted the congratulatory ceremony. The announcement to the temple, the texts for the six marriage gifts, and the rest of the ceremony were all settled by Biaozhi. On close examination the canonical forms prescribe the following. The proposing-gifts document, bearing the imperial seal, reads: "The emperor addresses the former staff officer of the Grand Commandant, He Qi: from the origin of primordial Heaven, when human relations were first ordered, down to husband and wife joined to serve Heaven and Earth, the ancestral temples, and the altars of soil and grain, the dukes and ministers were consulted, and all agreed that the old canon should be followed. We now send Minister of Ceremonies Biaozhi, bearer of credentials, and Director of the Imperial Clan Zong to present the proposing gifts according to ritual. " The host replies: "The emperor's gracious command seeks a bride from our humble house; the full rite of selection by proposing gifts is hereby acknowledged. My second cousin once removed, the late Gentleman of the Golden Saddle, Zhunzhi, left a daughter who is still young in training, of modest stature in dress and carriage; in reverent obedience to the old regulations and canonical order, she is offered for your choice. The former staff officer of the Grand Commandant, Marquis of Duxiang, your subject on humble soil, He Qi, kowtows twice and receives the imperial command. " The next ask-name document reads: "The emperor says: I address Official Such-and-Such of the Such-and-Such clan. Heaven and Earth joined in harmony sustain all things; she who is established within must come from a worthy house. Let the old canon be honored once more. We now send Minister of Ceremonies Such-and-Such, bearer of credentials, and Director of the Imperial Clan Such-and-Such to ask her name according to ritual. " The master of the house replied: "By the Emperor's gracious command, Envoy So-and-so has come and again reads the imperial edict, asking after my family name and lineage. The daughter of our clan, born to her parents, is the last surviving great-great-granddaughter of the late Lord Zhen, former Grand Minister of Splendid Brightness and Marquis of Yulou; the great-granddaughter of the late Lord Yun, former Inspector of Yuzhou and Marquis within the Passes; the granddaughter of the late Lord Rui, former Administrator of Anfeng and Marquis within the Passes; and the surviving daughter of the late Lord Zhun, former Attendant Cavalier-in-Ordinary. On her mother's side she counts as the maternal great-granddaughter of the late Lord Gou, former Left Vice Director of the Masters of Writing, and the maternal granddaughter of the late Lord Yi, former Palace Attendant and Marquis within the Passes. She is seventeen years old. I receive the ancient statutes with reverence and observe the canonical rites with solemn care. " Next came the board text for Accepting the Auspice: "The Emperor said: I consult the official of such rank and surname. Human counsel and the tortoise agree; all pronounce the match correct and auspicious. I shall reverently follow the canonical rite. I now send the Bearer of the Staff of Authority, the Director of Ceremonies So-and-so, and the Director of the Imperial Clan So-and-so to accept the auspice by ritual. " The master of the house replied: "By the Emperor's gracious command, Envoy So-and-so again reads the imperial edict. The Grand Diviner declares the match supremely auspicious. Our humble clan and low station are unworthy of such honor, and I am overwhelmed with anxiety and fear. I receive the ancient statutes with reverence and observe the canonical rites with solemn care. " Next came the board text for the Betrothal Gift: "The Emperor said: I consult the daughter of the official of such rank and surname. She has a mother's virtue, grace and modesty, steadfastness like mountains and rivers, and is fit to serve the ancestral temple and receive Heaven's mandate forever. Dark and light red silk, hides, silk, horses, sheep, cash, and jade disks are sent to display the canonical rite. I now send the Bearer of the Staff of Authority, the Minister over the Masses So-and-so, and the Director of Ceremonies So-and-so to deliver the betrothal gift by ritual. " The master of the house replied: "By the Emperor's gracious command, marriage is lowered to our humble house, yet raised with the rank of a Grand Duke, honored with canonical rite, and furnished with full ritual objects and written documents. I receive the ancient statutes with reverence and observe the canonical rites with solemn care. " Next came the board text for Setting the Date: "The Emperor said: I consult the official of such rank and surname. After counsel with dukes and ministers and divination with the great oracle and primordial tortoise, nothing is inauspicious. I shall fully follow the canonical rite. I now send the Bearer of the Staff of Authority, the Director of Ceremonies So-and-so, and the Director of the Imperial Clan So-and-so to set the date by ritual. " The master of the house replied: "By the Emperor's gracious command, Envoy So-and-so again reads the imperial edict. The auspicious day is such-and-such, when the bride may be received. I receive the ancient statutes with reverence and observe the canonical rites with solemn care. " Next came the board text for Welcoming the Bride in Person: "The Emperor said: I consult the official of such rank and surname. The year and month are auspicious, and the auspicious day is such-and-such. I shall follow ritual to welcome her. I now send the Bearer of the Staff of Authority, the Grand Tutor So-and-so, and the Grand Commander So-and-so to welcome her. " The master of the house replied: "By the Emperor's gracious command, Envoy So-and-so again reads the imperial edict. On this month's auspicious day and hour, all ritual is prepared to welcome her. Grand dukes and clan ministers arrive together with deputy envoys, and a hundred pairs of close retainers attend. Our clan is no more than ants, yet we undeservedly receive this great rite. Trembling with anxiety, I receive the ancient statutes with reverence and observe the canonical rites with solemn care. " Their prostrations in accepting the edict followed the same form as the first replies.
24
孝武納王皇后，其禮亦如之。 其納采、問名、納吉、請期、親迎，皆用白雁白羊各一頭，酒米各十二斛。 唯納徵羊一頭，玄纁用帛三匹，絳二匹，絹二百匹，虎皮二枚，錢二百萬，玉璧一枚，馬六頭，酒米各十二斛，鄭玄所謂五雁六禮也。 其珪馬之制，備物之數，校太康所奏，又有不同，官有其注。
When Emperor Xiaowu took Empress Wang, the same rites were followed. For Presenting the Gift, Inquiring the Name, Accepting the Auspice, Setting the Date, and Welcoming the Bride, each rite used one white wild goose and one white sheep, with twelve bushels each of wine and rice. Only the Betrothal Gift added one sheep, three bolts of dark and light red silk, two bolts of crimson silk, two hundred bolts of plain silk, two tiger hides, two million cash, one jade bi disk, six horses, and twelve bushels each of wine and rice—the "five geese and six rites" of Zheng Xuan. Regulations for jade scepters and horses and the tally of ritual objects differed again from the Taikang submission; the office keeps its own notes.
25
古者昏、冠皆有醮，鄭氏醮文三首具存。
In antiquity both marriage and capping included libation rites, and three libation texts by Zheng Xuan survive intact.
26
宋文帝元嘉十五年四月，皇太子納妃，六禮文與納后不異。 百官上禮。 其月壬戌，於太極殿西堂敍宴二宮隊主副、司徒征北鎮南三府佐、揚兗江三州綱、彭城江夏南譙始興武陵廬陵南豐七國侍郎以上，諸二千石在都邑者，並豫會。 又詔今小會可停妓樂，時有臨川曹太妃服。
In the fourth month of Yuanjia 15, when Emperor Wen of Song's crown prince took a consort, the texts for the six rites were the same as those for taking an empress. All officials presented congratulatory gifts. On renxu of that month a banquet was held in the West Hall of the Hall of Supreme Ultimate for the chief and deputy commanders of the two palaces' guards, aides of the Minister over the Masses and the Northern Expedition and Southern Suppression offices, commissioners of Yang, Yan, and Jiang, secretaries and above from the seven kingdoms of Pengcheng, Jiangxia, Nanqiao, Shixing, Wuling, Luling, and Nanfeng, and every two-thousand-bushel prefect then in the capital. An edict also suspended music and entertainers at this smaller gathering, because the Grand Consort Cao of Linchuan was then in mourning.
27
明帝泰始五年十一月，有司奏：「按晉江左以來，太子昏，納徵，禮用玉一，虎皮二，未詳何所準況。 或者虎取其威猛有彬炳，玉以象德而有溫潤。 尋珪璋既玉之美者，豹皮義兼炳蔚，熊羆亦昏禮吉徵，以類取象，亦宜並用，未詳何以遺文。 晉氏江左，禮物多闕，後代因襲，未遑研考。 今法章徽儀，方將大備。 宜憲範經籍，稽諸舊典。 今皇太子昏，納徵，禮合用珪璋豹皮熊羆皮與不？ 下禮官詳依經記更正。 若應用者，為各用一？ 為應用兩？ 」博士裴昭明議：「案周禮，納徵，玄纁束帛儷皮。 鄭玄注云：『束帛〔十端也。 儷，兩也。 兩皮為庭實，鹿皮也。 』晉太子納妃〕儀注，『以虎皮二』。 太元中，公主納徵，以虎豹皮各一具。 豈謂婚禮不辨王公之序，故取虎豹皮以尊革其事乎。 虎豹雖文，而徵禮所不用。 熊羆吉祥，而婚典所不及。 珪璋雖美，或為用各異。 今帝道弘明，徽則光闡，儲皇聘納，宜準經誥。 凡諸僻謬，並合詳裁。 雖禮代不同，文質或異，而鄭為儒宗，既有明說，守文淺見，蓋有惟疑。 兼太常丞孫詵議以為：『聘幣之典，損益惟義，歷代行事，取制士婚。 若珪璋之用，實均璧品，采豹之彰，義齊虎文，熊羆表祥，繁衍攸寄。 今儲后崇聘，禮先訓遠，皮玉之美，宜盡暉備。 禮稱束帛儷皮，則珪璋數合同璧，熊羆文豹，各應用二。 』長兼國子博士虞龢議：『案儀禮納徵，直云玄纁束帛雜皮而已。 禮記郊特牲云虎豹皮與玉璧，非虛作也。 則虎豹之皮，居然用兩，珪璧宜仍舊各一也。 』參詵、龢二議不異，今加珪璋各一，豹熊羆皮各二，以龢議為允。 」詔可。
In the eleventh month of Taishi 5, Emperor Ming, the relevant offices memorialized: "Since Eastern Jin, the crown prince's betrothal gift has used one jade and two tiger hides, but it is unclear what precedent this follows. Perhaps the tiger was chosen for fierce power and brilliant markings, and jade for virtue and warm luster. Gui and zhang are the finest jades; leopard hide is likewise splendid; bear and buffalo are also auspicious marriage emblems. By analogy they too should be used, yet the transmitted texts leave them out, and the reason is unclear. Eastern Jin lacked many ritual objects, and later ages inherited the gap without time to investigate. Now statutes and ceremonial insignia are to be fully restored. The classics should serve as model, and the old canons should be consulted. For the crown prince's marriage, should the betrothal gift include gui, zhang, leopard hide, and bear-and-buffalo hide? Let the ritual officers examine the classics and correct the practice in detail. If they are to be used, should there be one of each? Or should there be two of each? " Doctor Pei Zhaoming argued: "The Rites of Zhou says that the betrothal gift consists of dark and light red silk bundled with paired hides. Zheng Xuan comments: 'Bundled silk 〈missing in source〉 ten lengths. 'Paired' means two. Two hides serve as court offerings: deer hide. 〈missing in source〉 The Jin crown prince's consort-taking protocol reads: 'with two tiger hides.' In the Taiyuan era a princess's betrothal gift used one tiger hide and one leopard hide. Was this because marriage rites did not distinguish royal from ducal rank, and tiger and leopard hides were chosen to honor and elevate the occasion? Tiger and leopard may be splendidly marked, but they are not prescribed for the betrothal gift. Bear and buffalo are auspicious, yet the marriage canon does not include them. Gui and zhang are splendid, but their use may differ from case to case. Now the imperial way is broad and bright and ceremonial norms are clear; the heir apparent's betrothal should follow the classic injunctions. Every irregular deviation should be examined and decided in detail. Rites change from age to age and form and substance differ, yet Zheng Xuan is patriarch of the Ru school and his explanations are clear; shallow literalism only breeds doubt. The Director of Ceremonies Assistant Sun Shen also argued: 'Betrothal gifts may be increased or reduced only as righteousness requires. Each age in practice modeled itself on the scholar's marriage. Gui and zhang match bi disks in grade; the leopard's patterned glory parallels the tiger's markings; bear and buffalo express auspice and the hope of offspring. The heir's lofty betrothal, with ritual preceding instruction far and wide, should display the full splendor of hides and jade. Since the rites speak of bundled silk and paired hides, gui and zhang should match bi in number, and bear, buffalo, and patterned leopard should each be two. ' Chief and Concurrent Erudite of the Imperial Academy Yu He argued: 'The Etiquette and Ceremonial on the betrothal gift says only dark and light red silk bundled with assorted hides. The Records of Ritual, Sacrificial Victims, says tiger and leopard hide with jade bi—not an empty invention. Tiger and leopard hides are clearly used in pairs; gui and bi should remain one each, as before. ' Shen's and He's views agreed on the whole. Gui and zhang were added one each, and leopard, bear, and buffalo hide two each; Yu He's opinion was adopted. " The edict approved the proposal.
28
晉武帝泰始十年，將聘拜三夫人九嬪。 有司奏：「禮，皇后聘以穀珪，無妾媵禮贄之制。 」詔曰：「拜授可依魏氏故事。 」於是臨軒使使持節兼太常拜夫人，兼御史中丞拜九嬪。
In Taishi 10, Emperor Wu of Jin was about to betroth and invest three Ladies and nine Palatines. The relevant offices memorialized: "By ritual the empress is betrothed with a grain-patterned gui, and there is no prescribed gift for concubines and attendant ladies. " The edict said: "Investiture may follow Wei precedent. " Thereupon, facing the hall, he sent the Bearer of the Staff of Authority, who was also Director of Ceremonies, to invest the Ladies, and the Censor-in-Chief to invest the Palatines.
29
漢、魏之禮，公主居第，尚公主者來第成婚。 司空王朗以為不可，其後乃革。
Under Han and Wei ritual the princess kept her own residence, and the man who married her went there to complete the marriage. Grand Minister of Works Wang Lang judged this improper, and the practice was later changed.
30
凡遣大使拜皇后、三公，及冠皇太子，及拜蕃王，帝皆臨軒。 其儀，太樂令宿設金石四廂之樂於殿前。 漏上二刻，侍中、侍臣、冗從僕射、中謁者、節騎郎、虎賁，旄頭遮列，五牛旗皆入。 虎賁中郎將、羽林監分陛端門內。 侍御史、謁者各一人監端門。 廷尉監、平分陛東、西中華門。 漏上三刻，殿中侍御史奏開殿之殿門、南止車門、宣陽城門。 軍校、侍中、散騎常侍、給事黃門侍郎、散騎侍郎升殿夾御座。 尚書令以下應階者以次入。 治禮引大鴻臚入，陳九賓。 漏上四刻，侍中奏：「外辦。 」皇帝服袞冕之服，升太極殿，臨軒南面。 謁者前北面一拜，跪奏：「大鴻臚臣某稽首言，羣臣就位。 謹具。 」侍中稱制曰：「可。 」謁者贊拜，在位皆再拜。 大鴻臚稱臣一拜，仰奏：「請行事。 」侍中稱制曰：「可。 」鴻臚舉手曰：「可行事。 」謁者引護當使者當拜者入就拜位。 四廂樂作。 將拜，樂止。 禮畢出。 官有其注。
Whenever great envoys were sent to invest the empress, the Three Excellencies, the crown prince at his capping, or feudal kings, the Emperor always faced the hall in person. In the ceremony the Director of Music set out the four-sided metal-and-stone ensemble before the hall the night before. At the second clepsydra mark after midnight, Palace Attendants, attending ministers, supernumerary Masters of Horse, Central Ushers, Staff Horse Lieutenants, and Tiger Braves entered with plumed-head guards screening the ranks, and all Five-Ox banners entered. The Commandant of Tiger Braves and the Superintendent of the Forest Guard took their posts at the inner steps and End Gate. One Supervising Censor and one Usher each kept watch at the End Gate. Prison Superintendents A and B took the eastern and western steps at Zhonghua Gate. At the third clepsydra mark the Attending Censor in the Hall reported the opening of the Hall Gate, the South Halting-Chariot Gate, and the Xuanyang City Gate. Military adjutants, Palace Attendants, Regular Palace Attendants, Attendant Masters of Writing of the Yellow Gate, and Attendant Masters of Writing entered the hall and flanked the imperial seat. The Director of the Masters of Writing and all who were to ascend the steps entered in order. The Master of Ritual Conduct led the Grand Master of Ceremonies in and arranged the Nine Guests. At the fourth clepsydra mark the Palace Attendant reported: "All external preparations are complete. " The Emperor put on the robe and cap of state, ascended the Hall of Supreme Ultimate, and sat facing south at the hall front. " The Usher stepped forward, bowed once facing north, knelt, and reported: "Grand Master of Ceremonies, your subject So-and-so, prostrate, reports that the ministers are all in place. Everything has been prepared with care. " The Palace Attendant announced the imperial decision: "Proceed. " The Usher called for the bow, and all present bowed twice. The Grand Master of Ceremonies bowed once as subject, raised his head, and reported: "I request permission to perform the rite. " The Palace Attendant announced the imperial decision: "Proceed. " The Grand Master of Ceremonies raised his hand and said: "The rite may begin. " The Usher guided the escorts, envoys, and appointees to their places for the bow. The four-sided ensemble began to play. Just before the bow, the music stopped. When the rite was finished, they withdrew. The office keeps its own notes on the ceremony.

舊時歲旦，常設葦茭桃梗，磔雞於宮及百寺門，以禳惡氣。 漢儀，則仲夏之月設之，有桃卯，無磔雞。 案明帝大修禳禮，故何晏禳祭議據雞牲供禳釁之事，磔雞宜起於魏也。 桃卯本漢所以輔，卯金又宜魏所除也，但未詳改仲夏在歲旦之所起耳。 宋皆省，而諸郡縣此禮往往猶存。
In old times at the New Year reed, rush, and peach branches were set out and chickens were dismembered at the palace and at the gates of the hundred temples to drive off evil vapors. Han practice set them out in midsummer; there were peach pegs, but no chicken dismemberment. Since Emperor Ming greatly restored exorcism rites, He Yan's discussion of exorcism sacrifice cites chicken victims for exorcism and blood-smearing; dismembering chickens probably began under Wei. Peach charms and mao branches were Han additions to the rite; mao and the Metal phase were rightly dropped under Wei—yet when the ceremony moved from midsummer to New Year's Day remains unclear. The Song court abolished the practice entirely, though in many commanderies and counties the old rite still lingered.

上代聘享之禮，雖頗見經傳，然首尾不全。 叔孫通傳載通所制漢元會儀，綱紀粗舉，施於今，又未周備也。 魏國初建，事多兼闕，故黃初三年，始奉璧朝賀。 何承天云，魏元會儀無存者。 案何楨許都賦曰：「元正大饗，壇彼西南。 旗幕峨峨，檐宇弘深。 」王沈正會賦又曰：「華幄映於飛雲，朱幕張于前庭。 絙青帷於兩階，象紫極之崢嶸。 延百辟于和門，等尊卑而奉璋。 」此則大饗悉在城外，不在宮內也。 臣案魏司空王朗奏事曰：「故事，正月朔，賀。 殿下設兩百華鐙，對於二階之間。 端門設庭燎火炬，端門外設五尺、三尺鐙。 月照星明，雖夜猶晝矣。 」如此，則不在城外也。 何、王二賦，本不在洛京。 何云許都賦，時在許昌也。 王賦又云「朝四國於東巡」，亦賦許昌正會也。
Earlier protocols for embassies and tribute appear here and there in the classics, but never in a complete account from start to finish. Shusun Tong's biography preserves the Han New Year's audience he devised—only a rough outline—and even by the present day the rite remained incomplete. Wei in its founding years left much undone; not until Huangchu 3 did the court first present jade and receive New Year's homage. He Chengtian notes that no record of Wei's New Year's audience survives. He Zhen's Rhapsody on the Capital at Xu reads: "On New Year's Day the grand feast is held; the altar stands in the southwest. Banners and pavilions rise in lofty rows; eaves and halls stretch wide and deep. Wang Shen's Rhapsody on the Proper Audience adds: "Splendid canopies gleam against the flying clouds; crimson curtains open across the forecourt. Azure curtains span the twin stairways, evoking the lofty majesty of the Purple Apex. The hundred ministers gather at the Gate of Harmony, high and low alike bearing jade tablets in tribute. By these accounts the grand feast was held entirely outside the walls, not within the palace. Your subject finds in a memorial by Wang Lang, Minister of Works under Wei: "By established precedent, on the first day of the first month homage is paid. Two hundred decorated lamps are placed beneath the hall, facing one another between the twin stairways. Court braziers and torches are lit at the Main Gate, and outside it lamps of five and three feet are arranged. Moon and stars blaze so brightly that night becomes as day. On this evidence the ceremony was not held outside the walls. Neither He's nor Wang's rhapsody originally described Luoyang. He titled his work the Rhapsody on the Capital at Xu, for the court was then at Xuchang. Wang's poem likewise speaks of "receiving the four states on the eastern progress"—another account of Xuchang's formal New Year's audience.

晉武帝世，更定元會注，今有咸寧注是也。 傅玄元會賦曰：「考夏后之遺訓，綜殷、周之典藝，採秦、漢之舊儀，定元正之嘉會。 」此則兼採眾代可知矣。 咸寧注，先正月一日，守宮宿設王公卿校便坐於端門外，大樂鼓吹又宿設四廂樂及牛馬帷閤於殿前。 夜漏未盡十刻，羣臣集到，庭燎起火。 上賀謁報，又賀皇后。 還從雲龍東中華門入謁，詣東閤下便坐。 漏未盡七刻，羣司乘車與百官及受贄郎下至計吏，皆入，詣陛部立。 其陛衞者，如臨軒儀。 漏未盡五刻，謁者僕射、大鴻臚各奏：「羣臣就位定。 」漏盡，侍中奏：「外辦。 」皇帝出。 鍾鼓作，百官皆拜伏。 太常導皇帝升御座。 鍾鼓止。 百官起。 大鴻臚跪奏：「請朝賀。 」治禮郎讚：「皇帝延王登。 」大鴻臚跪讚：「蕃王臣某等奉白璧各一，再拜賀。 」太常報：「王悉登。 」謁者引上殿，當御座。 皇帝興，王再拜。 皇帝坐，復再拜，跪置璧御座前，復再拜。 成禮訖，謁者引下殿，還故位。 治禮郎引公、特進、匈奴南單于子、金紫將軍當大鴻臚西，中二千石、二千石、千石、六百石當大行令西，皆北面伏。 大鴻臚跪讚：「太尉、中二千石等奉璧皮帛羔雁雉，再拜賀。 」太常讚：「皇帝延君登。 」治禮引公至金紫將軍上殿，當御座。 皇帝興，皆再拜。 皇帝坐，又再拜。 跪置璧皮帛御座前，復再拜。 成禮訖，讚者引下殿，還故位。 王公置璧成禮時，大行令並讚，殿下中二千石以下同。 成禮訖，以贄授受贄郎，郎以璧帛付謁者，羔雁雉付太官。 太樂令跪請奏雅樂。 以次作樂。 乘黃令乃出車。 皇帝罷入，百官皆坐。 晝漏上水六刻，諸蠻夷胡客以次入，皆再拜訖，坐。 御入三刻，又出。 鍾鼓作。 謁者僕射跪奏：「請羣臣上。 」謁者引王公至二千石上殿，千石、六百石停本位。 謁者引王詣尊酌壽酒，跪授侍中。 侍中跪置御座前。 王還自酌，置位前。 謁者跪奏：「蕃王臣某等奉觴再拜，上千萬歲壽。 」侍中曰：「觴已上。 」百官伏稱萬歲。 四廂樂作。 百官再拜。 已飲，又再拜。 謁者引諸王等還本位。 陛者傳就席，羣臣皆跪諾。 侍中、中書令、尚書令各於殿上上壽酒，登歌樂升，太官令又行御酒。 御酒升階，太官令跪授侍郎，侍郎跪進御座前。 乃行百官酒。 太樂令跪奏：「奏登歌。 」三。 終，乃降。 太官令跪請御飯到陛，羣臣皆起。 太官令持羹跪授司徒； 持飯跪授大司農； 尚食持案並授侍郎，侍郎跪進御座前。 羣臣就席。 太樂令跪奏：「食。 舉樂。 」太官行百官飯案遍。 食畢，太樂令跪奏：「請進儛。 」儛以次作。 鼓吹令又前跪奏：「請以次進眾伎。 」乃召諸郡計吏前，授敕戒於階下。 宴樂畢，謁者一人跪奏：「請罷退。 」鍾鼓作，羣臣北面再拜出。 江左更隨事立位，大體亦無異也。 宋有天下，多仍舊儀，所損益可知矣。
Under Emperor Wu of Jin the New Year's audience was re-regulated; the Xianning commentary that survives is that revision. Fu Xuan's Rhapsody on the New Year's Audience says: "Drawing on Xia's surviving teachings, weighing the canonical arts of Yin and Zhou, and collecting Qin and Han precedent, he established the great assembly of New Year's Day. This shows plainly that the rite combined practices from many ages. The Xianning commentary begins: On the first day of the first month, the palace guard spends the night arranging folding seats outside the Main Gate for kings, dukes, ministers, and senior officials; the Directorate of Music and Drum-and-Pipe office likewise prepare music on four sides and ox-and-horse pavilions before the hall. Before ten night watches remain on the clepsydra, the ministers assemble and the court braziers are kindled. The emperor pays his respects and receives the formal reply, then offers New Year's congratulations to the empress. He returns by the eastern Zhonghua Gate of the Cloud Dragon Gate to pay homage, then takes a folding seat beneath the eastern pavilion. With seven watches still remaining, officials of every office arrive by carriage, together with all ranks down to tribute attendants and accounting clerks, and take their places at the foot of the steps. The step guards observe the same protocol used for an audience at the front hall. With five watches left, the Chief Usher and Grand Master of Ceremonies each report: "The assembled ministers are in position. When the clepsydra empties, the Attendant Within reports: "All is ready outside. The emperor then comes forth. Bells and drums strike; every official bows to the ground. The Minister of Ceremonies guides the emperor up to the imperial throne. The bells and drums fall silent. The officials rise. The Grand Master of Ceremonies kneels and petitions: "We beg to begin the New Year's audience. The Director of Ritual calls out: "The emperor invites the kings to ascend. The Grand Master of Ceremonies kneels and announces: "The feudal kings, your subjects So-and-so and the rest, each present one white jade disc and bow twice in congratulation. The Minister of Ceremonies replies: "Let all the kings ascend. Ushers lead them up the hall to stand before the throne. The emperor stands; the kings bow twice. When the emperor is seated they bow again, kneel to set the jade before the throne, and bow twice more. Once the ceremony is finished, the usher conducts them down the hall and back to their places. The Director of Ritual places dukes, specially advanced officials, the son of the Southern Xiongnu Chanyu, and gold-seal generals with purple cords west of the Grand Master of Ceremonies, and middle-second-rank officials through sixth-rank salary west of the Director of Great Processions—all facing north and prostrate. The Grand Master of Ceremonies kneels and announces: "The Grand Commandant, middle-second-rank officials, and the rest present jade, leather, silk, lambs, geese, and pheasants, and bow twice in congratulation. The Minister of Ceremonies calls: "The emperor invites you, my lords, to ascend. The Director of Ritual leads the dukes through the gold-seal generals up the hall to stand before the throne. The emperor rises; all bow twice. When he is seated they bow twice again. They kneel, set the jade and silk offerings before the throne, and bow twice more. After the ceremony the announcer leads them down the hall and back to their stations. While kings and dukes presented their jade, the Director of Great Processions joined in the announcements; below the hall, middle-second-rank officials and those beneath them did likewise. Once the ceremony ended, the tribute gifts went to the receiving attendants, who passed jade and silk to the ushers and the lambs, geese, and pheasants to the Director of the Palace Kitchen. The Director of Music kneels and asks that court music be played. The music is performed in turn. The Director of Imperial Carriages then has the chariots brought out. The emperor retires within, and the officials all take their seats. At the sixth watch of the day clepsydra, barbarian and foreign guests enter in succession, each bowing twice before taking a seat. Three watches into the emperor's withdrawal, he comes out again. Bells and drums strike once more. The Chief Usher kneels and petitions: "We beg the assembled ministers to ascend. Ushers conduct kings, dukes, and second-rank officials up the hall, while first-rank and sixth-rank officials remain at their posts. An usher guides a king to the place of honor to pour longevity wine, kneels, and presents it to the Attendant Within. The Attendant Within kneels and sets it before the throne. The king withdraws, pours for himself, and places the cup before his own seat. An usher kneels and announces: "The feudal kings, your subjects So-and-so and the rest, raise the cup, bow twice, and wish ten thousand years of life. The Attendant Within declares: "The cup has been offered. All officials prostrate and cry, "Ten thousand years!" Music rises from all four sides. The officials bow twice. After drinking, they bow twice again. Ushers conduct the kings and the rest back to their places. Attendants at the steps pass the order to be seated, and the ministers kneel in assent. The Attendant Within, Director of the Secretariat, and Director of the Department of State Affairs each offer longevity wine in the hall; the ascending song begins, and the Director of the Palace Kitchen serves the emperor's wine. The imperial wine is carried up the steps; the Director of the Palace Kitchen kneels and passes it to a Vice Director, who kneels and presents it before the throne. Wine is then served to all the officials. The Director of Music kneels and reports: "Play the ascending song. Three times. When the performance ends, the musicians descend. The Director of the Palace Kitchen kneels to announce that the imperial meal has reached the steps, and all the ministers rise. The Director of the Palace Kitchen holds the soup, kneels, and presents it to the Minister of Education; holds the rice, kneels, and presents it to the Minister of Revenue; and the Director of Imperial Cuisine carries the tray and, together with a Vice Director, kneels to present it before the throne. The ministers take their seats. The Director of Music kneels and announces: "While the meal is taken, let music be raised." The Director of the Palace Kitchen sends meal trays to every official in turn. When the meal is finished, the Director of Music kneels and petitions: "We beg that the dancers be brought in. The dances are performed one after another. The Director of Drum-and-Pipe likewise steps forward, kneels, and asks: "We beg that the various performers enter in turn. The accounting clerks from every commandery are then called forward and receive the emperor's charge and admonition at the foot of the steps. When the banquet and music are complete, a single usher kneels and petitions: "We beg leave to withdraw. Bells and drums sound; the ministers turn north, bow twice, and depart. South of the Yangzi positions were adjusted case by case, yet the overall form differed little. Once Song held the empire it mostly retained the old ceremonies, and the additions and cuts are plain enough.

魏制，蕃王不得朝覲。 明帝時有朝者，皆由特恩，不得以為常。 晉泰始中，有司奏：「諸侯之國，其王公以下入朝者，四方各為二番，三歲而周，周則更始。 若臨時有故，却在明年。 來朝之後，更滿三歲乃復，不得從本數。 朝禮執璧如舊朝之制。 不朝之歲，各遣卿奉聘。 」奏可。 江左王侯不之國，其有授任居外，則同方伯刺史二千石之禮，亦無朝聘之制，此禮遂廢。
Wei law forbade feudal kings from coming to court for audience. Those who appeared at court under Emperor Ming did so only by special favor and could not be treated as precedent. During Jin's Taishi reign, officials submitted a memorial: princes and lesser lords coming to court from the four quarters should each take two turns, completing the full round in three years; when the round was finished, the count would start again. If an unforeseen circumstance arose at the appointed time, the visit could be postponed to the following year. After a court visit, another full three years had to pass before one might come again; the original schedule could not be resumed. The court audience rite, with the presentation of a bi jade, was to follow the former court-visit regulations. In years when a lord did not attend in person, each state was to send a minister bearing a courtesy mission. The memorial was approved. In the south, princes and marquises no longer took up their fiefs; those posted abroad were treated like regional inspectors and two-thousand-shi prefects, and the court-visit and courtesy-mission system likewise lapsed—so the rite fell out of use.

正旦元會，設白虎樽於殿庭。 樽蓋上施白虎，若有能獻直言者，則發此樽飲酒。 案禮記，知悼子卒，未葬，平公飲酒，師曠、李調侍，鼓鍾。 杜蕢自外來，聞鍾聲曰：「安在？ 」曰：「在寢。 」杜蕢入寢，歷階而升，酌曰：「曠飲斯。 」又酌曰：「調飲斯。 」又酌，堂上北面坐飲之，降，趨而出。 平公呼而進之曰：「蕢，曩者爾心或開予，是以不與爾言。 爾飲曠，何也？ 」曰：「子卯不樂，知悼子在堂，斯其為子卯也大矣。 曠也，太師也。 不以詔，是以飲之也。 」「爾飲調，何也？ 」曰：「調也，君之褻臣也。 為一飲一食，忘君之疾，是以飲之也。 」「爾飲，何也？ 」曰：「蕢也宰夫，唯刀匕是供，又敢與知防，是以飲也。 」平公曰：「寡人亦有過焉。 酌而飲寡人。 」杜蕢洗而揚觶。 公謂侍者曰：「如我死，則必無廢斯爵。 」至于今，既畢獻，斯揚觶，謂之「杜舉」。 白虎樽，蓋杜舉之遺式也。 畫為虎，宜是後代所加，欲令言者猛如虎，無所忌憚也。
At the New Year's grand assembly, a White Tiger goblet was placed in the palace courtyard. A white tiger was mounted on the lid; if someone wished to speak blunt truth, this goblet was opened and wine drunk from it. The Book of Rites records that when Zhi Daozi died and had not yet been buried, Duke Ping was drinking wine while Shi Kuang and Li Diao attended and bells were struck. Du Kui came in from outside, heard the bells, and asked, "Where is he?" They answered, "In the inner chamber." Du Kui entered the chamber, climbed the steps, poured wine, and said, "Kuang, drink this." He poured again and said, "Diao, drink this." He poured once more, sat facing north in the hall and drank, then went down the steps and hurried out. Duke Ping called him back and said, "Kui, earlier I thought your heart was open to me, and so I did not speak with you." "Why did you make Kuang drink?" He replied, "On the days of zi and mao one does not make music; with Zhi Daozi's body still in the hall, this was a day of zi and mao in the fullest sense." Kuang is the Grand Music Master. He was not admonished, and for that I made him drink. "Why did you make Diao drink?" He replied, "Diao is your intimate attendant. For one cup and one meal he forgot your grief, and for that I made him drink." "And why did you drink?" He replied, "I, Kui, am only a cook who supplies knives and spoons; yet I dared to share in guarding against impropriety, and for that I drank." Duke Ping said, "I too have been at fault. Pour and make me drink." Du Kui washed the cup and raised it high. The duke told his attendants, "When I die, you must never let this cup fall out of use." Down to the present, after the offering is complete, raising the cup aloft is called "Du's Toast." The White Tiger goblet was likely a surviving form of Du's Toast. Painting it as a tiger was probably a later addition, meant to make speakers as fierce as tigers, without fear or restraint.

漢以高帝十月定秦旦為歲首，至武帝雖改用夏正，然朔猶常饗會，如元正之儀。 魏、晉則冬至日受萬國及百僚稱賀，因小會。 其儀亞於歲旦，晉有其注。 宋永初元年八月，詔曰：「慶冬使或遣不，事役宜省，今可悉停。 唯元正大慶，不得廢耳。 郡縣遣冬使詣州及都督府者，亦宜同停。」
Han began with Gaozu's tenth-month new year, taken from Qin; though Wu later adopted the Xia calendar, the new-moon feast still followed the New Year's rites. Under Wei and Jin, the winter solstice brought congratulations from all the realms and the hundred officials, followed by a lesser court gathering. The ceremony ranked below New Year's Day; Jin preserved detailed notes on it. In the eighth month of Song's first Yongchu year, an edict declared: "Winter-solstice envoys need not always be sent; public labor should be reduced, and such missions may now all be suspended. Only the great New Year's celebration must not be abandoned. Winter-solstice envoys sent from counties and districts to prefectures and regional command posts should likewise be stopped."

孫權始都武昌及建業，不立郊兆。 至末年太元元年十一月，祭南郊，其地今秣陵縣南十餘里郊中是也。 晉氏南遷，立南郊於巳地，非禮所謂陽位之義也。 宋孝武大明三年九月，尚書右丞徐爰議：「郊祀之位，遠古蔑聞。 禮記『燔柴於泰壇，祭天也。 』『兆於南郊，就陽位也。 』漢初甘泉河東禋埋易位，終亦徙於長安南北。 光武紹祚，定二郊洛陽南北。 晉氏過江，悉在北。 及郊兆之議，紛然不一。 又南出道狹，未議開闡，遂於東南巳地創立丘壇。 皇宋受命，因而弗改。 且居民之中，非邑外之謂。 今聖圖重造，舊章畢新，南驛開塗，陽路修遠。 謂宜移郊正午，以定天位。 」博士司馬興之、傅郁、太常丞陸澄並同爰議。 乃移郊兆於秣陵牛頭山西，正在宮之午地。 世祖崩，前廢帝即位，以郊舊地為吉祥，移還本處。
When Sun Quan first ruled from Wuchang and Jiankang, he did not establish suburban altars. Near the end of his reign, in the eleventh month of Taixi 1, he sacrificed at the southern suburb; the site lies at Jiao Zhong, more than ten li south of present-day Moling County. After the Jin crossed south, they placed the southern suburb in the si direction—not the yang position that ritual prescribed. In the ninth month of Xiaowu's third Daming year, Xu Ai, Right Assistant Director of the Masters of Writing, argued: "The site of suburban sacrifice is nowhere recorded in deepest antiquity. The Book of Rites says, "Burning firewood on the great mound is sacrifice to Heaven. Establishing the altar at the southern suburb means taking the yang position." In early Han the Ganquan and Hedong suburban rites shifted sites repeatedly; in the end they were fixed north and south of Chang'an. When Guangwu restored the dynasty, he fixed the two suburban altars north and south of Luoyang. After the Jin crossed the Yangtze, all the altars lay to the north. Debates over the suburban altars produced many conflicting views. The southern road was too narrow and had not yet been widened, so a mound altar was created in the southeast at the si position. When Song received the Mandate, it kept the arrangement unchanged. Moreover, placing the altar among inhabited ground was not what ritual meant by "outside the city." Now the sacred realm has been rebuilt, old regulations fully renewed, the southern post road opened, and the yang road cleared and extended. The suburban altar should be moved to true south at the wu position, thereby fixing Heaven's place." The academicians Ma Xingzhi and Fu Yu, and Lu Cheng, Assistant Director of the Grand Master of Ceremonies, all agreed with Xu Ai. The suburban altar was then moved west of Mount Niutou in Moling, directly on the palace's southern wu axis. After Emperor Shizu died and the Deposed Emperor succeeded, he took the old suburban site to be auspicious and moved the altar back.
39
北郊，晉成帝世始立，本在覆舟山南。 宋太祖以其地為樂游苑，移於山西北。 後以其地為北湖，移於湖塘西北。 其地卑下泥濕，又移於白石邨東。 其地又以為湖，乃移於鍾山北原道西，與南郊相對。 後罷白石東湖，北郊還舊處。
The northern suburb was first established under Jin's Emperor Cheng, originally south of Mount Fuzhou. Song's Emperor Taizu turned the site into the Leyou Garden and moved the northern altar to the northwest of the mountain. Later, when that ground became North Lake, the altar was moved to the northwest of the lake embankment. The ground there was low and wet, so it was moved again to the east of Baishi Village. When that site too became a lake, the altar was moved west of the road on the northern plain of Mount Zhong, opposite the southern suburb. Later, when Baishi East Lake was drained, the northern suburb returned to its former site.
40
南郊，皇帝散齋七日，致齋三日。 官掌清者亦如之。 致齋之朝，御太極殿幄坐。 著絳紗袍，黑介幘，通天金博山冠。 先郊日未晡五刻，夕牲。 公卿京兆尹眾官悉壇東就位，太祝史牽牲入。 到榜，稟犧令跪白：「請省牲。 」舉手曰：「腯。 」太祝令繞牲，舉手曰：「充。 」太祝令牽牲詣庖。 以二陶豆酌毛血，其一奠皇天神座前，其一奠太祖神座前。 郊之日未明八刻，太祝令進饌，郎施饌。 牲用璽栗二頭，羣神用牛一頭。 醴用秬鬯，藉用白茅。 玄酒一器，器用匏陶，以瓦樽盛酒，瓦圩斟酒。 璧用蒼玉。 蒯席各二，不設茵蓐。 古者席藁，晉江左用蒯。 車駕出，百官應齋及從駕填街先置者，各隨申攝從事。 上水一刻，御服龍袞，平天冠，升金根車，到壇東門外。 博士、太常引入到黑攢。 太祝令跪執匏陶，酒以灌地。 皇帝再拜，興。 羣臣皆再拜伏。 治禮曰：「興。 」博士、太常引皇帝至南階，脫舄升壇，詣罍盥。 黃門侍郎洗爵，跪授皇帝。 執樽郎授爵，酌秬鬯授皇帝。 跪奠皇天神座前，再拜，興。 次詣太祖配天神座前，執爵跪奠，如皇天之禮。 南面北向，一拜伏。 太祝令各酌福酒，合置一爵中，跪進皇帝，再拜伏。 飲福酒訖，博士、太常引帝從東階下，還南階。 謁者引太常升壇，亞獻。 謁者又引光祿升壇，終獻。 訖。 各降階還本位。 太祝送神，跪執匏陶，酒以灌地。 興。 直南行出壇門，治禮舉手白，羣臣皆再拜伏。 皇帝盤，治禮曰：「興。 」博士跪曰：「祠事畢，就燎。 」博士、太常引皇帝就燎位，當壇東階，皇帝南向立。 太祝令以案奉玉璧牲體爵酒黍飯諸饌物，登柴壇施設之。 治禮舉手曰：「可燎。 」三人持火炬上。 火發。 太祝令等各下壇。 壇東西各二十人，以炬投壇，火半柴傾。 博士仰白：「事畢。 」皇帝出便坐。 解嚴。 天子有故，則三公行事，而太尉初獻，其亞獻、終獻，猶太常、光祿勳也。 北郊齋、夕牲、進熟，及乘輿百官到壇三獻，悉如南郊之禮； 唯事訖，太祝令牲玉饌物詣埳置牲上訖，又以一牲覆其上。 治禮舉手曰：「可埋。 」二十人俱時下土。 填埳欲半，博士仰白：「事畢。 」帝出。 自魏以來，多使三公行事，乘輿罕出矣。 魏及晉初，儀注雖不具存，所損益漢制可知也。 江左以後，官有其注。
For the southern suburb rite, the emperor kept preliminary abstinence for seven days and strict abstinence for three. Officials responsible for purification did the same. On the morning of strict abstinence, he took the screened seat in the Hall of Supreme Ultimate. He wore a crimson gauze robe, a black kerchief cap, and the Tongtian golden Boshan crown. On the eve of the sacrifice, five watches before sunset, the evening victim rite was performed. Grandees, the Governor of Jingzhao, and all officials took their places east of the altar while the Grand Invocator's clerk led the victim in. At the placard they reported to the Sacrificial Victim Director, who knelt and said, "I request to inspect the victim." Raising his hand, he declared, "Fat." The Grand Invocator circled the victim and, raising his hand, said, "Full." The Grand Invocator then led the victim to the kitchen. With two pottery dou vessels he ladled hair and blood, placing one before the seat of August Heaven and the other before the Founding Ancestor's seat. On the day of the sacrifice, eight watches before dawn, the Grand Invocator brought forward the offerings and the attendants arranged them. The principal victim was two dappled chestnut horses; for the host of spirits, one ox. The sweet wine was ju chang; the matting was white thatch grass. There was one vessel of dark water; gourd pottery was used for vessels, earthenware goblets held the wine, and earthenware ladles poured it. The bi disc was of pale green jade. There were two cattail mats each, with no padded cushions beneath. In antiquity straw mats were used; in Jin south of the Yangtze they used cattail mats. When the imperial procession set out, fasting officials and those already lining the streets each took up their acting assignments and followed. One watch into the water hour, the emperor put on the dragon robe and Pingshan crown, mounted the golden-root chariot, and reached the east gate of the altar. The academicians and the Grand Master of Ceremonies led him to the black enclosure. The Grand Invocator knelt, took the gourd pottery vessel, and poured wine to libate the ground. The emperor bowed twice and rose. All the ministers bowed twice and prostrated themselves. The Director of Ritual called, "Rise." The academicians and Grand Master of Ceremonies led the emperor to the southern steps; he removed his shoes, climbed the altar, and went to the urn to wash his hands. The Gentleman Attendant of the Yellow Gate washed the goblet and knelt to present it to the emperor. The cup-bearer handed over the goblet, poured ju chang, and presented it to the emperor. The emperor knelt and placed it before the seat of August Heaven, bowed twice, and rose. Next he went to the Founding Ancestor's seat paired with Heaven, held the goblet, knelt, and offered it with the same rite as to August Heaven. Facing south with his back to the north, he bowed once and prostrated himself. The Grand Invocator ladled the blessing wine from each offering, combined it in one goblet, knelt, and presented it; the emperor bowed twice and prostrated himself. After drinking the blessing wine, the academicians and Grand Master of Ceremonies led the emperor down the eastern steps and back to the southern steps. The usher led the Grand Master of Ceremonies up the altar for the secondary offering. The usher then led the Director of the Imperial Household up the altar for the final offering. The rite was complete. Each descended the steps and returned to his place. The Grand Invocator sent off the spirits, knelt, took the gourd pottery vessel, and poured wine to libate the ground. Rise.
