He walked due south out through the altar gate. The Director of Ritual raised his hand and gave the call, and every minister bowed twice and prostrated. The emperor remained prostrate. The Director of Ritual said, "Rise." The academician knelt and said, "The rite is finished. Proceed to the burning." The academician and Grand Master of Ceremonies led the emperor to the burning station at the eastern steps of the altar, where he stood facing south. The Grand Invocator bore the jade bi, sacrificial meat, goblets, wine, millet, rice, and the rest of the offerings on trays, climbed the firewood altar, and set them out. The Director of Ritual raised his hand and called, "Begin the burning." Three torchbearers climbed the altar. The fire caught. The Grand Invocator and the others each came down from the altar. Twenty men on the east and twenty on the west of the altar threw torches onto it; when the blaze was half gone, the stack of firewood gave way. The academician looked up and announced, "The rite is complete." The emperor withdrew to the informal seat. The guard was stood down. When the Son of Heaven was prevented from attending, the Three Excellencies performed the rite: the Grand Commandant made the first offering, and the secondary and final offerings still fell to the Grand Master of Ceremonies and the Director of the Imperial Household. At the northern suburb, abstinence, the evening victim, the presentation of the cooked offering, and the arrival of the imperial carriage and officials at the altar for the three libations all followed the southern suburb rite. Only at the end, the Grand Invocator carried the victim, jade, and offerings to the pit, laid the victim on top, and then covered it with a second victim. The Director of Ritual raised his hand and called, "Begin the burial." Twenty men all at once began shoveling earth. When the pit was nearly half full, the academician looked up and announced, "The rite is complete." The emperor withdrew. From Wei times onward, the Three Excellencies were often sent to perform the rites in the emperor's place, and the Son of Heaven himself seldom went out. Under Wei and early Jin, though the full ritual code did not survive, one can still see how Han practice had been altered. After the court moved south of the Yangtze, the offices kept written regulations for the rites.
41
魏文帝詔曰：「漢氏不拜日於東郊，而旦夕常於殿下東面拜日，煩褻似家人之事，非事天郊神之道也。 」黃初二年正月乙亥，朝日于東門之外。 按禮，天子以春分朝日於東，秋分夕月於西，今正月，非其時也。 漢郊祀志，帝郊泰畤，平旦出竹宮東向揖日，其夕西向揖月。 此為即用郊日，不俟二分也。 明帝太和元年二月丁亥朔，朝日于東郊，八月己丑，夕月于西郊，此古禮也。 白虎通：「王者父天、母地，兄日、姊月」，此其義也。 尚書大傳，迎日之詞曰：「維某年某月上日。 明光于上下，勤施于四方，旁作穆穆，維予一人。 某敬拜迎日于郊。 」吳時郎陳融奏東郊頌，吳時亦行此禮也。 晉武帝太康二年，有司奏：「春分依舊請車駕祀朝日，寒溫未適，可不親出。 」詔曰：「禮儀宜有常； 如所奏，與故太尉所撰不同，復為無定制。 間者方難未平，故每從所奏。 今戎事弭息，唯此為大。 」案此詔，帝復為親朝日也。 此後廢。
Emperor Wen of Wei decreed: "The Han never worshipped the sun at the eastern suburb, yet morning and evening they bowed to the sun beneath the palace, facing east—fussy and domestic, like household business, not the proper way to serve Heaven and the suburban spirits." On yihai day in the first month of Huangchu 2, he worshipped the sun outside the eastern gate. According to the Rites, the Son of Heaven worships the sun in the east at the spring equinox and the moon in the west at the autumn equinox; the first month was not the proper season. The Han Treatise on Suburban Sacrifice records that at the Tai suburban altar the emperor left the bamboo palace at dawn and bowed to the sun facing east, and in the evening bowed to the moon facing west. That meant performing the rite on the day of the suburban sacrifice itself, without waiting for the equinoxes. On dinghai, the first day of the second month in Taihe 1, Emperor Ming worshipped the sun at the eastern suburb; on jichou in the eighth month he worshipped the moon at the western suburb—the ancient rite restored. The White Tiger Discourse says, "The king takes Heaven as father, Earth as mother, the sun as elder brother, and the moon as elder sister"—that is the principle behind the rite. The Great Commentary on the Documents gives the words for welcoming the sun: "In such-and-such year, in such-and-such month, on the first day." Brightness fills heaven and earth; diligent bounty reaches the four quarters; all around there is solemn harmony—I alone am here." So-and-so reverently bows and welcomes the sun at the suburb." In Wu, Gentleman Chen Rong submitted an Eastern Suburb Eulogy; Wu too observed this rite. In Taikang 2, Emperor Wu's officials memorialized: "At the spring equinox, as in former practice, the imperial carriage should worship the sun; the weather may not yet be suitable—the emperor might not need to go out in person." The edict replied: "Ritual ought to be constant. As you propose, that would differ from what the late Grand Commandant compiled, and again there would be no fixed rule. While the realm's troubles were not yet settled, I always followed such memorials. Now that war has ceased, this alone is the greater matter." From this edict one can see that the emperor again went in person to worship the sun. After that the rite was abandoned.
42
殷祠，皇帝散齋七日，致齋三日。 百官清者亦如之。 致齋之日，御太極殿幄坐，著絳紗袍，黑介幘，通天金博山冠。 祠之日，車駕出，百官應齋從駕留守填街先置者，各依宣攝從事。 上水一刻，皇帝著平冕龍袞之服，升金根車，到廟北門訖。 治禮、謁者各引太樂、太常、光祿勳、三公等皆入在位。 皇帝降車入廟，脫舄，盥及洗爵，訖，升殿。 初獻，奠爵，樂奏。 太祝令跪讀祝文，訖，進奠神座前，皇帝還本位。 博士引太尉亞獻，訖，謁者又引光祿勳終獻。 凡禘祫大祭，則神主悉出廟堂，為昭穆以安坐，不復停室也。 晉氏又有陰室四殤，治禮引陰室以次奠爵于饌前。 其功臣配饗者，設坐於庭，謁者奠爵于饌前。 皇帝不親祠，則三公行事，而太尉初獻，太常亞獻，光祿勳終獻也。 四時祭祀，亦皆於將祭必先夕牲，其儀如郊。
For the regular temple sacrifice, the emperor kept preliminary abstinence for seven days and strict abstinence for three days. Purified officials did the same. On the day of strict abstinence he sat in the curtained seat in the Hall of Supreme Ultimate, wearing a deep-red gauze robe, black headband, and the Tongtian crown with its golden Boshan finial. On the day of the sacrifice, when the imperial procession set out, fasting officials followed; those left behind to line the streets and those sent ahead each took up their acting assignments. One watch into the water hour, the emperor donned the flat crown and dragon robe, mounted the golden-root chariot, and reached the north gate of the temple. The Director of Ritual and the ushers led the Director of Music, Grand Master of Ceremonies, Director of the Imperial Household, Three Excellencies, and the rest to their places. The emperor descended, entered the temple, removed his shoes, washed his hands, and washed the goblet; then he ascended the hall. At the first offering he set down the goblet, and music sounded. The Grand Invocator knelt and read the prayer; when he finished, he advanced and placed the offering before the spirit seat, and the emperor returned to his place. The academician led the Grand Commandant in the secondary offering; when that was done, the usher led the Director of the Imperial Household in the final offering. At the great di and xia sacrifices, all the spirit tablets were brought out into the temple hall and seated in zhao-mu order, no longer kept in the side chambers. Jin also had the shade chamber for the four infant spirits; the Director of Ritual led offerings from the shade chamber in turn to set goblets before the food. Meritorious ministers granted a place at the feast were seated in the courtyard, and ushers set goblets before the offerings. When the emperor did not sacrifice in person, the Three Excellencies performed the rite: the Grand Commandant made the first offering, the Grand Master of Ceremonies the second, and the Director of the Imperial Household the third. The seasonal sacrifices likewise required presenting the victim on the eve of the rite, following the suburban pattern.
43
晉武帝泰始七年四月，帝將親祠，車駕夕牲，而儀注還不拜。 詔問其故。 博士奏：「歷代相承如此。 」帝曰：「非致敬宗廟之禮也。 」於是實拜而還，遂以為制。 太康中，有司奏議，十一月一日合朔奠、冬烝、夕牲同日，可有司行事。 詔曰：「夕牲而令有司行事，非也。 改擇上旬他日。 」案此則武帝夕牲必躬臨拜，而江左以來復止也。 晉元帝建武元年三月辛卯，即晉王位，行天子殷祭之禮，非常之事也。 孝武太元十一年九月，皇女亡及應烝祠。 中書侍郎范甯奏：「案喪服傳，有死宮中者，三月不舉祭，不別長幼之與貴賤也。 皇女雖在嬰孩，臣竊以為疑。 」於是尚書奏使三公行事。 昔漢靈帝世，立春尚齋迎氣東郊，尚書左丞毆殺陌使於南書寺，於是詔書曰：「議郎蔡邕、博士任敏，問可齋祠不？ 得無不宜？ 」邕等對曰：「按上帝之祠，無所為廢。 宮室至大，陌使至微，日又寬，可齋無疑。 」甯非不知有此議，然不從也。 魏及晉初，祭儀雖不具存，江左則備矣。 官有其注。
In the fourth month of Taishi 7, when Emperor Wu was about to sacrifice in person, the imperial carriage went for the evening victim, but the ritual code prescribed no bow on returning. An edict asked why. The academicians replied: "Successive ages have handed it down this way." The emperor said, "That is not the rite for showing reverence to the ancestral temple." He then bowed in earnest on returning, and that became the rule. In the Taikang era, officials memorialized that on the first day of the eleventh month the new-moon offering, the winter xia sacrifice, and the evening victim all fell on the same day, and proposed that officials perform the rite. The edict said, "To present the evening victim and then have officials perform the rite is wrong. Choose another day in the first ten days of the month." From this one can see that Emperor Wu always went in person to bow at the evening victim, whereas after the move south of the Yangtze the practice again lapsed. On ximao in the third month of Jianwu 1, when Emperor Yuan took the throne of Jin, he performed the Son of Heaven's regular temple sacrifice—an extraordinary act. In the ninth month of Taiyuan 11, Emperor Xiaowu's daughter died just as the winter xia sacrifice was due. Palace Secretary Fan Ning memorialized: "The Commentary on Mourning Garb says that when someone dies within the palace, sacrifices are suspended for three months, without distinction of age or rank." Though the imperial daughter was still an infant, I privately find this doubtful." The Ministry of Works then memorialized that the Three Excellencies should perform the rite. Under Emperor Ling of Han, at the spring establishment, while the Director of Works was fasting to welcome the qi at the eastern suburb, the Left Assistant Director of the Ministry of Works beat and killed a roadside messenger at the Southern Archive Office. An edict then asked: "Consultation Gentlemen Cai Yong and Academician Ren Min—may fasting and sacrifice proceed? Might there be anything improper?" Might there be anything unsuitable?" Yong and the others replied: "For the sacrifice to August Heaven, nothing should cause it to be suspended. The palace is vast, the roadside messenger utterly insignificant, and the day is ample—fasting may proceed without doubt." Ning can hardly have been unaware of this precedent, yet he did not follow it. Under Wei and early Jin the sacrificial rites were not fully preserved, but south of the Yangtze they were complete. The offices had regulations for them.
44
祠太社、帝社、太稷，常以歲二月八月二社日祠之。 太祝令夕牲進熟，如郊廟儀。 司空、太常、大司農三獻也。 官有其注。 周禮王親祭，漢以來，有司行事。
The Grand Altar of the State, the Emperor's Altar of the State, and the Grand Altar of the Grain-God were sacrificed to on the two She days of the second and eighth months each year. The Grand Invocator presented the evening victim and the cooked offering, following the suburban and temple pattern. The Minister of Works, Grand Master of Ceremonies, and Minister of Grand Agriculture made the three offerings. The offices had regulations for this as well. The Rites of Zhou prescribe that the king sacrifice in person; from Han onward, officials performed the rite.
45
漢安帝元初六年，立六宗祠於國西北戌亥地，祠儀比泰社。
In Yuanchu 6 of Emperor An of Han, six ancestral spirit temples were established in the xu-hai sector northwest of the capital; the rite matched that of the Grand Altar of the State.
46
日月將交會，太史上合朔。 尚書先事三日，宣攝內外，戒嚴。 摯虞決疑曰：「凡救蝕者，皆著赤幘，以助陽也。 日將蝕，天子素服避正殿，內外嚴警，太史登靈臺，伺候日變。 更伐鼓於門，聞鼓音，侍臣皆著赤幘，帶劍入侍。 三臺令史以上，皆各持劍立其戶前。 衞尉卿馳繞宮，伺察守備，周而復始。 日復常，乃皆罷。 」魯昭公十七年，六月朔，日有蝕之。 祝史請所用幣，叔孫昭子曰：「日有蝕之，天子不舉樂，伐鼓於社； 諸侯用幣於社，伐鼓於朝，禮也。 」又以赤絲為繩繫社，祝史陳辭以責之。 社，勾龍之神，天子之上公，故責之。 合朔，官有其注。
When the sun and moon were about to meet in conjunction, the Grand Astrologer reported the new moon. Three days beforehand the Ministry of Works issued orders throughout the inner and outer courts and imposed strict guard. Zhi Yu's Resolving Doubts says: "All who respond to an eclipse wear red headcloths to assist the yang." When the sun is about to be eclipsed, the Son of Heaven wears plain garments and withdraws from the main hall; inside and outside the court is placed on strict alert; the Grand Astrologer ascends the Spirit Terrace and watches for changes in the sun. The drum is changed and beaten at the gate; at the sound, attendants all wear red headcloths, gird on swords, and enter to attend. Clerks of the Three Offices and above each hold a sword and stand before their doors. The Commandant of the Guards rides circuit around the palace, inspecting the defenses, and repeats the round. When the sun returned to normal, all were dismissed. In the seventeenth year of Duke Zhao of Lu, on the first day of the sixth month, there was an eclipse of the sun. The invocator and clerk asked what offerings should be used. Shusun Zhaozi said: "When the sun is eclipsed, the Son of Heaven stops music and beats the drum at the altar of the soil. Feudal lords use silks at the altar of the soil and beat the drum at court—that is the rite." They also made a cord of red silk and bound it to the altar, and the invocator and clerk pronounced words of rebuke. The altar of the soil is the spirit Goulong, the Son of Heaven's upper duke—hence he rebukes it. For the new-moon conjunction, the offices had regulations.
47
昔漢建安中，將正會，而太史上言正旦當日蝕，朝士疑會不。 共詣尚書令荀文若諮之。 時廣平計吏劉劭在坐，曰：「梓慎、裨竈，古之良史，猶占水火，錯失天時。 禮諸侯旅見天子，入門不得終禮者四，日蝕在一。 然則聖人垂制，不為變異豫廢朝禮者，或災消異伏，或推術謬誤也。 」文若及眾人咸喜而從之，遂朝會如舊，日亦不蝕。 劭由此顯名，魏史美而書之。
In Han times during the Jian'an era, when a grand assembly was about to be held, the Grand Astrologer reported a solar eclipse on New Year's Day, and court gentlemen doubted whether the assembly should proceed. Together they went to consult the Minister of Works, Xun Wenruo. Liu Shao, a Guangping accounting clerk, was among those present. He said, "Zi Shen and Bi Zao were the finest historians of old, yet even when they read fire and water they still mistimed Heaven." The Book of Rites holds that when lords arrived in turn for audience with the Son of Heaven, four circumstances could prevent the rite from being finished once they had passed the gate; a solar eclipse was one. The sages laid down these rules and did not cancel court ceremony in advance because of portents—either the disaster never came and the omen vanished, or the astronomers' calculations were wrong. Wen Ruo and the rest were delighted and agreed. The court assembly went ahead as usual, and in the end the sun was not eclipsed. Shao won renown from the affair, and the Wei histories commended it in their annals.
48
魏高貴鄉公正元二年三月朔，太史奏日蝕而不蝕。 晉文王時為大將軍，大推史官不驗之負。 史官答曰：「合朔之時，或有日掩月，或有月掩日。 月掩日，則蔽障日體，使光景有虧，故謂之日蝕。 日掩月，則日於月上過，謂之陰不侵陽，雖交無變。 日月相掩必食之理，無術以知，是以嘗禘郊社，日蝕則接祭，是亦前代史官不能審蝕也。 自漢故事，以為日蝕必當於交。 每至其時，申警百官，以備日變。 故甲寅詔有備蝕之制，無考負之法。 古來黃帝、顓頊、夏、殷、周、魯六歷，皆無推日蝕法，但有考課疏密而已。 負坐之條，由本無術可課，非司事之罪。 」乃止。
On the first day of the third month in Zhengyuan 2, under the Wei emperor at Gaoguixiang, the Grand Clerk reported an eclipse of the sun that never happened. Sima Zhao, then Grand General and later Jin Wen Wang, pressed hard to hold the court astronomers accountable for the failed prediction. The historians answered, "At new moon, either the sun may pass over the moon, or the moon may pass before the sun. When the moon covers the sun, it blocks the solar disk and dims the light—that is what we call a solar eclipse. When the sun covers the moon, the sun simply passes above it. This is called yin not encroaching on yang: though the bodies meet, nothing visible changes. There is no reliable method to know in advance whether a mutual covering of sun and moon must produce an eclipse. That is why, at the great di and the suburban sacrifices to soil and grain, a predicted eclipse did not halt the rite—earlier court astronomers could not judge eclipses with certainty either. Han practice assumed that any solar eclipse would fall at new moon. Each time that moment came, the court warned every office to stand ready for a change in the sun. The Jia-yin edict therefore provided measures against eclipses, but no statute for investigating failure and assigning blame. From antiquity onward, the six calendars of Huangdi, Zhuanxu, Xia, Yin, Zhou, and Lu had no method for predicting solar eclipses—only rules for judging whether work was tight or slack. The clause on punishment existed because there had never been a method by which to test them; it was not the fault of the officials responsible. The inquiry was dropped.
49
晉武帝咸寧三年、四年，並以正旦合朔却元會，改魏故事也。
In Xianning 3 and 4 under Jin Emperor Wu, new moon on New Year's Day led both years to cancel the New Year's grand assembly, overturning the Wei precedent.
50
晉元帝太興元年四月合朔，中書侍郎孔愉奏曰：「春秋日有蝕之，天子伐鼓于社，攻諸陰也。 諸侯伐鼓於朝，臣自攻也。 案尚書符，若日有變，便伐鼓於諸門，有違舊典。 」詔曰：「所陳有正義，輒敕外改之。」
At new moon in the fourth month of Taixing 1 under Jin Emperor Yuan, Palace Attendant Kong Yu submitted a memorial: "When the Spring and Autumn Annals says the sun was eclipsed, the Son of Heaven beats the drum at the altar of soil to strike at the yin force. Feudal lords beat the drum in court—the ministers, in effect, strike at themselves." But under the Secretariat directive, any solar anomaly at once sent drums beating at every gate. That departs from the old canon." The edict replied, "Your point is just. Order the outer offices to change the practice at once."
51
至康帝建元元年，太史上元日合朔，朝士復疑應却會與否。 庾冰輔政，寫劉劭議以示八坐，于時有謂劭為不得禮意，荀文若從之，是勝人之一失。 故蔡謨遂著議非之曰：「劭論災消異伏，又以慎、竈猶有錯失，太史上言亦不必審，其理誠然也。 而云聖人垂制，不為變異豫廢朝禮，此則謬矣。 災祥之發，所以譴告人君，王者所重誡。 故素服廢樂，退避正寢，百官降物，用幣伐鼓，躬親而救之。 夫敬誡之事，與其疑而廢之，寧慎而行之。 故孔子、老聃助葬於巷黨，以喪不見星而行，故日蝕而止柩，曰安知其不見星也。 今史官言當蝕，亦安知其不蝕乎？ 夫子、老聃豫行見星之防，而劭廢之，是棄聖賢之成規也。 魯桓公壬申有災，而以乙亥嘗祭，春秋譏之。 災事既過，猶追懼未已，故廢宗廟之祭； 況聞天眚將至，行慶樂之會，於禮乖矣。 禮記所云『諸侯入門不得終禮者』，謂日官不豫言，諸侯既入，見蝕乃知耳； 非先聞當蝕，而朝會不廢也。 劭引此，可謂失其義指。 劉劭所執者禮記也； 夫子、老聃巷黨之事，亦禮記所言，復違而反之，進退無據。 荀令所善，漢朝所從，遂使此言至今見稱，莫知其謬。 後來君子，將擬以為式，故正之云爾。 」於是冰從眾議，遂以却會。
In Jianyuan 1 under Emperor Kang, the Grand Clerk reported new moon on New Year's Day, and court officials again debated whether the assembly should be cancelled. Regent Yu Bing copied out Liu Shao's argument for the Eight Dignitaries. Some at the time said Shao had missed the point of ritual, yet Xun Wenruo had followed him—that was one mistake of the victorious faction. Cai Mo then wrote a rebuttal: "Shao said calamities may fade and omens vanish, and that even Zi Shen and Bi Zao erred—that the Grand Clerk's warning need not be trusted. On that much he is right. But to claim that the sages laid down rites and therefore never cancelled court ceremony in advance because of portents—that is wrong. Calamities and omens arise to warn and rebuke the ruler. They are what a king must treat with the gravest heed. Hence plain dress, music stopped, withdrawal from the principal chamber, officials lowering their insignia, silks offered and drums beaten—the ruler himself moves to answer the warning. In matters of reverent warning, it is better to act with caution than to hesitate and abandon the rite. Confucius and Laozi once helped with a burial in the lanes. A funeral should not proceed unless stars can be seen, so when a solar eclipse came they halted the coffin, saying, Who can know that the stars will not appear? Now the astronomers say there will be an eclipse—who can know that there will not be one? The Master and Laozi took precautions against the chance that stars might not be seen, yet Shao would discard that caution. That is to throw away the settled rule of the sages. Duke Huan of Lu suffered a calamity on the day ren-shen, yet held the seasonal sacrifice on yi-hai—the Spring and Autumn Annals censures him for it. Even after the disaster had passed, fear still lingered, and so the ancestral sacrifice was cancelled. How much less, then, when heaven's scourge is known to be coming, should one hold a joyous celebratory assembly. That violates ritual. When the Book of Rites speaks of lords entering the gate and being unable to finish the rite, it means the Clerk of the Sun had not spoken in advance—the lords were already inside and only learned of the eclipse when they saw it. It does not mean hearing beforehand that an eclipse was expected and still refusing to cancel the court assembly. Shao's citation misses the point entirely. Liu Shao appealed to the Book of Rites. The story of the Master and Laozi in the lanes is also in the Book of Rites—yet he turned against that passage too. In argument he had nowhere firm to stand. What Commandant Xun approved and the Han court followed has been praised ever since, though few see the error in it. Later gentlemen may take it as precedent, and so I set the record straight. Yu Bing then sided with the majority and cancelled the assembly.
52
至永和中，殷浩輔政，又欲從劉劭議不却會。 王彪之據咸寧、建元故事，又曰：「禮云，諸侯旅見天子，不得終禮而廢者四，自謂卒暴有之，非為先存其事而徼幸史官推術繆錯，故不豫廢朝禮也。 」於是又從彪之，相承至今。
In the Yonghe era, regent Yin Hao again wanted to follow Liu Shao and keep the assembly. Wang Biaozhi, citing the Xianning and Jianyuan precedents, argued again: "Ritual says that when lords come in turn to audience, four circumstances may force the rite to be abandoned. That refers to sudden, unforeseen events—not to keeping the assembly scheduled while gambling that the astronomers miscalculated, and therefore not cancelling court ceremony in advance. The court again followed Biaozhi, and that practice has continued to the present.
53
耕籍之禮尚矣，漢文帝修之。 及昭帝幼即大位，耕於鈎盾弄田。 明帝永平十五年二月，東巡，耕於下邳。 章帝元和三年正月北巡，耕於懷縣。 魏三祖皆親耕籍。 晉武帝泰始四年，有司奏始耕祠先農，可令有司行事。 詔曰：「夫民之大事，在祀與農。 是以古之聖王，躬耕帝籍，以供郊廟之粢盛，且以訓化天下。 近代以來，耕籍止於數步中，空有慕古之名，曾無供祀訓農之實，而有百官車徒之費。 今修千畝之制，當與羣公卿士，躬稼穡之艱難，以帥先天下。 主者詳具其制，并下河南處田地於東郊之南，洛水之北，平良中水者。 若無官田，隨宜便換，不得侵民人也。 」自此之後，其事便廢。 史注載多有闕。 江左元、哀二帝，將修耕籍，賀循等所上注，及裴憲為胡中所定儀，又未詳允。
The rite of plowing the sacred field is very old. Emperor Wen of Han revived it. When Emperor Zhao came to the throne as a child, he plowed in the Hook Shield pleasure field. In the second month of Yongping 15, Emperor Ming toured east and plowed at Xiapi. In the first month of Yuanhe 3, Emperor Zhang toured north and plowed in Huai county. All three Wei founding emperors plowed the sacred field in person. In Taishi 4 under Jin Emperor Wu, officials proposed that the opening plowing and sacrifice to the First Farmer could be carried out by the responsible offices. The edict said, "The people's greatest concerns are sacrifice and farming. That is why the sage kings of old plowed the imperial field themselves, to supply the grain for suburban and temple offerings and to teach the realm by example. In recent times the plowing has amounted to a few steps in the field—a show of reverence for antiquity with none of the substance of supplying sacrifice or teaching farming, yet still costing the labor of countless officials and attendants. Let the thousand-mu system be restored. Together with the high ministers I shall feel the hardship of sowing and reaping, and lead the realm by going first. The responsible office shall draw up the full regulations and set aside fields in Henan south of the eastern suburb and north of the Luo River, on level, fertile ground with adequate water. If no official land is available, substitute other land as convenient, but private holdings must not be seized. After that the practice lapsed. The historical commentaries leave much unrecorded. South of the Yangzi, under Emperors Yuan and Ai, when the court wished to restore plowing the sacred field, the notes submitted by He Xun and others, and the rites Pei Xian fixed for the northern tribes, were still incomplete and unsatisfactory.
54
元嘉二十年，太祖將親耕，以其久廢，使何承天撰定儀注。 史學生山謙之已私鳩集，因以奏聞。 乃下詔曰：「國以民為本，民以食為天。 一夫輟耕，饑者必及。 食廪既實，禮節以興。 自頃在所貧耗，家無宿積，陰陽暫偏，則人懷愁墊； 年或不稔，而病乏比室。 誠由政德未孚，以臻斯弊，抑亦耕桑未廣，地利多遺。 宰守微化導之方，萌庶忘勤分之義。 永言弘濟，明發載懷。 雖制令亟下，終莫懲勸，而坐望滋殖，庸可致乎。 有司其班宣舊條，務盡敦課。 遊食之徒，咸令附業。 考覈勤惰，行其誅賞； 觀察能殿，嚴加黜陟。 古者從時脉土，以訓農功，躬耕帝籍，敬供粢盛。 仰瞻前王，思遵令典，便可量處千畝，考卜元辰。 朕當親率百辟，致禮郊甸。 庶幾誠素，獎被斯民。 」於是斟酌眾條，造定圖注。 先立春九日，尚書宣攝內外，各使隨局從事。 司空、大農、京尹、令、尉，度宮之辰地八里之外，整制千畝，開阡陌。 立先農壇於中阡西陌南，御耕壇於中阡東陌北。 將耕，宿設青幕于耕壇之上。 皇后帥六宮之人出穜稑之種，付籍田令。 耕日，太祝以一太牢告祠先農，悉如祠帝社之儀。 孟春之月，擇上辛後吉亥日，御乘耕根三蓋車，駕蒼駟，青旂，著通天冠，青幘，朝服青袞，帶佩蒼玉。 蕃王以下至六百石皆衣青。 唯三臺武衞不耕，不改服章。 車駕出，眾事如郊廟之儀。 車駕至籍田，侍中跪奏：「尊降車。 」臨壇，大司農跪奏：「先農已享，請皇帝親耕。 」太史令讚曰：「皇帝親耕。 」三推三反。 於是羣臣以次耕，王公五等開國諸侯五推五反，孤卿大夫七推七反，士九推九反。 籍田令率其屬耕，竟畝，灑種，即耰，禮畢。
In Yuanjia 20 the founding emperor planned to plow in person. Because the rite had long fallen into disuse, he ordered He Chengtian to draft the ceremonial regulations. The historical student Shan Qianzhi had already compiled a private draft, which he submitted for the purpose. An edict followed: "The state rests on the people; the people rest on food. When one man leaves the plow, hunger reaches others. When the granaries are full, rites and decorum flourish. Lately every region has grown poor and drained; households keep no reserve grain. When yin and yang fall briefly out of balance, people sink into despair. Some years fail to ripen, and want and sickness spread from house to house. This truly comes of government whose virtue has not yet won trust, and so these ills have grown—but also because farming and mulberry culture are not widely practiced and much of the land's bounty goes unused. Local governors give little thought to how they should teach and guide; common people forget their duty to labor diligently. I speak constantly of broad relief, and from dawn my mind is heavy with the burden. Though edicts go out again and again, no one is moved to reform. Yet to sit idle and expect abundance—how can that come to pass? Let the responsible offices publish the old statutes and enforce them with full diligence. All drifters and idlers shall be made to take up settled work. Review diligence and laziness, and apply reward and punishment. Observe who excels and who falls short, and promote or dismiss with strictness. In antiquity rulers read the seasons and tested the soil to teach farming, plowed the imperial field in person, and reverently supplied sacrificial grain. Looking back to the kings of old, I mean to follow their canon: let a thousand mu be measured and set aside, and an auspicious day be chosen by divination. I shall lead the hundred officials in person and perform the rites in the suburban field. May sincerity and plain living be honored and spread among the people. The court then weighed the various provisions and completed the diagrams and annotations. Nine days before Establishment of Spring, the Masters of Writing announced oversight throughout the court, and each office was to attend according to its charge. The Minister of Works, Grand Minister of Agriculture, Capital Intendant, magistrates, and commandants, measuring eight li from the palace's southeast quarter, laid out the thousand mu and opened the field paths. They built the First Farmer altar south of the central west path and the imperial plowing altar north of the central east path. On the eve of plowing, a green canopy was erected over the plowing altar. The empress led the women of the six palaces to bring out fine and coarse seed and handed them to the Director of the Sacred Field. On plowing day the Grand Invoker sacrificed to the First Farmer with one taolao, following exactly the rite used for the God of Soil. In the first month of spring, on an auspicious hai day after upper xin, the emperor rode the three-canopied Root-Plowing carriage, drawn by grey-black horses under a green banner, wearing the Through-Heaven cap, green kerchief, green court robe, belt, and blue-green jade. From feudal kings down to officials of six hundred shi, all wore green. Only the Three Departments and the military guard did not plow and kept their usual dress and insignia. When the imperial procession set out, every detail followed suburban and temple ceremony. When the carriage reached the sacred field, the Attendant-in-Ordinary knelt and announced, "Your Majesty, please descend from the carriage." At the altar the Grand Minister of Agriculture knelt and said, "The First Farmer has received sacrifice. We ask that Your Majesty plow in person." The Director of Astronomy intoned, "The emperor plows in person." Three furrows forward and three back. Then the ministers plowed in order: kings and dukes of the fifth rank and founding marquises, five furrows and five returns; solitary ministers and grand masters, seven and seven; gentlemen, nine and nine. The Director of the Sacred Field led his staff to finish the field, scatter seed, cover it at once, and complete the rite.
55
魏氏雖天子耕籍，其蕃鎮諸侯，並闕百畝之禮。 晉武帝末，有司奏：「古諸侯耕籍百畝，躬秉耒耜，以奉社稷宗廟，以勸率農功。 今諸王治國，宜修耕籍之義。 」然未施行。 宋太祖東耕後，乃班下州郡縣，悉備其禮焉。
Although the Wei emperors plowed the sacred field, their feudal lords in their domains all omitted the hundred-mu rite. Near the end of Jin Emperor Wu's reign, officials submitted a memorial: "In antiquity feudal lords plowed a hundred mu of the sacred field, personally holding plow and spade, to supply the altars of soil and grain and the ancestral temples and to encourage farming. The princes who govern their states should now restore the meaning of plowing the sacred field. Yet the measure was never carried out. After Song Taizu performed the eastern plowing ceremony, the rite was promulgated to every commandery, prefecture, and county, each fully observing it.
56
周禮，王后帥內外命婦，蠶於北郊。 漢則東郊，非古也。 魏則北郊，依周禮也。 晉則西郊，宜是與籍田對其方也。 魏文帝黃初七年正月，命中宮蠶于北郊。 按韋誕后蠶頌，則于時漢注已亡，更考撰其儀也。 及至晉氏，先蠶多采魏法。 晉武帝太康六年，散騎常侍華嶠奏：「先王之制，天子諸侯親耕千畝，后夫人躬蠶桑宮。 今陛下以聖明至仁，修先王之緒，皇后體資生之德，合配乾之義，而教道未先，蠶禮尚闕。 以為宜依古式，備斯盛典。 」詔曰：「古者天子親籍以供粢盛，后夫人躬蠶以備祭服。 所以聿遵孝敬，明教示訓也。 今籍田有制，而蠶禮不修。 中間務多，未暇崇備。 今天下無事，宜修禮以示四海。 其詳依古典及近代故事，以參今宜。 明年施行。 」於是使侍中成粲草定其儀。 皇后采桑壇在蠶室西，帷宮中門之外，桑林在其東，先蠶壇在宮外門之外而東南。 取民妻六人為蠶母。 蠶將生，擇吉日，皇后著十二笄，依漢魏故事，衣青衣，乘油蓋雲母安車，駕六馬。 女尚書著貂蟬，佩璽，陪乘，載筐鉤。 公主、三夫人、九嬪、世婦、諸太妃、公太夫人、公夫人，及縣鄉君、郡公侯特進夫人、外世婦、命婦，皆步搖、衣青，各載筐鉤從。 蠶桑前一日，蠶宮生蠶著薄上。 躬桑日，太祝令以一太牢祠先蠶。 皇后至西郊，升壇，公主以下陪列壇東。 皇后東面躬桑，采三條； 諸妃公主各采五條； 縣鄉君以下各采九條。 悉以桑授蠶母。 還蠶室。 事訖，皇后還便坐，公主以下以次就位，設饗賜絹各有差。 宋孝武大明四年，又修此禮。
The Rites of Zhou prescribe that the queen lead the palace ladies and appointed wives to raise silkworms at the northern suburb. The Han used the eastern suburb—a departure from antiquity. Wei restored the northern suburb, in accord with the Rites of Zhou. Jin chose the western suburb, likely to mirror the sacred plowing field across the compass. In the first month of the seventh year of Huangchu, Emperor Wen of Wei ordered the inner palace to raise silkworms at the northern suburb. Wei Dan\'s ode on the queen\'s silkworm rite shows that by then the Han commentaries were lost and the ceremony had to be reconstructed from scratch. Under the Jin, the Prior Silkworm rite largely followed Wei precedent. In the sixth year of Taikang, Attendant Cavalier Hua Qiao submitted a memorial: "By the ordinance of the ancient kings, the Son of Heaven and feudal lords personally plow the sacred thousand mu, and the queen and principal consort personally tend silkworms at the palace mulberry grove. Your Majesty, in sage brilliance and deepest benevolence, continues the work of the ancient kings; the empress embodies the nurturing virtue of Heaven\'s creative power—yet moral instruction has not been set first, and the silkworm rite remains neglected. It would be fitting to follow the ancient pattern and restore this grand ceremony. The emperor replied: "In antiquity the Son of Heaven personally plowed the sacred field to supply sacrificial grain, and the queen and principal consort personally raised silkworms to provide vestments for the altars. This was how filial reverence was earnestly upheld and moral instruction plainly shown. Today the plowing-field rite is regulated, yet the silkworm ceremony goes unobserved. Pressing affairs in the intervening years left no time to restore it fully. Now that the realm is at peace, the rite should be restored as an example to all under Heaven. Draw the details from classical sources and recent precedent, adapting them to present needs. It shall be carried out next year. Attendant-in-Ordinary Cheng Can was charged with drafting the ceremonial regulations. The empress\'s mulberry-picking altar stood west of the silkworm chamber, with a curtained pavilion outside the inner gate; the mulberry grove lay to the east, and the Prior Silkworm altar southeast of the outer gate. Six commoner wives were appointed Silkworm Mothers. When the silkworms were about to hatch, on an auspicious day the empress wore twelve hairpins, and following Han and Wei custom donned green robes and rode a lacquered-canopy carriage with mica inlay, drawn by six horses. The Lady Director, wearing her diao and chan insignia and bearing the seal, rode alongside her carrying mulberry baskets and picking hooks. Princesses, the Three Ladies, the Nine Concubines, hereditary consorts, imperial grand consorts, ducal grand ladies, ducal ladies, county and township noblewomen, wives of distinguished lords, external consorts, and appointed wives all wore swaying step headdresses and green robes, each carrying baskets and hooks in procession. On the eve of the ceremony, newly hatched silkworms from the silkworm palace were laid out on trays. On the day of the empress\'s mulberry picking, the Grand Invoker sacrificed a full ta lao to the Prior Silkworm. The empress came to the western suburb and ascended the altar; princesses and those of lower rank stood in attendance on the east side. Facing east, the empress personally picked three mulberry branches; imperial consorts and princesses each picked five; county and township noblewomen and those below each picked nine. All the mulberry was given to the Silkworm Mothers. They then returned to the silkworm chamber. When the rite was complete, the empress returned to her seat; princesses and those below took their places in order, and a feast was held with silk gifts graded by rank. In the fourth year of Daming, Emperor Xiaowu of Song restored the ceremony once more.
57
漢獻帝建安二十二年，魏國作泮宮于鄴城南。 魏文帝黃初五年，立太學於洛陽。 齊王正始中，劉馥上疏曰：「黃初以來，崇立太學，二十餘年，而成者蓋寡。 由博士選輕，諸生避役，高門子弟，恥非其倫，故無學者。 雖有其名，而無其實，雖設其教，而無其功。 宜高選博士，取行為人表，經任人師者，掌教國子。 依遵古法，使二千石以上子孫，年從十五，皆入太學。 明制黜陟，陳榮辱之路。 」不從。 晉武帝泰始八年，有司奏：「太學生七千餘人，才任四品，聽留。 」詔：「已試經者留之，其餘遣還郡國。 大臣子弟堪受教者，令入學。 」咸寧二年，起國子學，蓋周禮國之貴遊子弟所謂國子，受教於師氏者也。 太康五年，修作明堂、辟雍、靈臺。
In the twenty-second year of Jian\'an, Wei built a Pan Palace south of Ye. In the fifth year of Huangchu, Emperor Wen of Wei founded the Imperial Academy at Luoyang. During the Zhengshi reign, Liu Fu submitted a memorial: "Since Huangchu the Imperial Academy has been honored and maintained, yet for more than twenty years scarcely anyone has completed its course. Erudites were chosen too casually; students enrolled to evade labor service; sons of great houses were ashamed to keep such company—so almost no one truly studied. It bore the name without the substance; teaching was established without effect. Choose Erudites of the highest caliber—men whose conduct sets the standard and whose command of the classics qualifies them to teach—and put them in charge of instructing the crown prince\'s sons. Follow the ancient law: all sons and grandsons of officials ranked two thousand shi and above, from age fifteen, should enter the Imperial Academy. Make promotion and demotion explicit, marking clear paths of honor and shame. His advice was not heeded. In the eighth year of Taishi, officials reported: "The Imperial Academy holds more than seven thousand students; those whose talents fit fourth-rank appointment may remain. The emperor replied: "Those who have passed the classics examination may stay; the rest shall be sent home to their commanderies and kingdoms. Sons of great ministers fit for instruction shall be enrolled. In the second year of Xianning the National University was founded—the school for noble scions called "sons of the realm" in the Rites of Zhou, who were taught by the royal tutor. In the fifth year of Taikang the Bright Hall, the Royal Academy, and the Spirit Terrace were constructed.
58
孫休永安元年，詔曰：「古者建國，教學為先。 所以導世治性，為時養器也。 自建興以來，時事多故，吏民頗以目前趨務，棄本就末，不循古道。 夫所尚不淳，則傷化敗俗。 其按舊置學官，立五經博士，覈取應選，加其寵祿。 科見吏之中及將吏子弟有志好者，各令就業。 一歲課試，差其品第，加以位賞。 使見之者樂其榮，聞之者羨其譽。 以淳王化，以隆風俗。 」於是立學。
In the first year of Yong\'an, Sun Xiu issued an edict: "In founding a state, education comes first. This guides the age, shapes character, and nurtures talent for the times. Since Jianxing affairs have been turbulent; officials and commoners alike chase immediate gain, abandoning fundamentals for frills and straying from the ancient path. When what is valued lacks purity, culture suffers and custom collapses. Restore school officials as before, appoint Erudites for the Five Classics, examine and select candidates rigorously, and increase their stipends and honors. Among serving officials and sons of officers who show aptitude and desire to learn, let each pursue his studies. Hold yearly examinations, grade students by rank, and grant office and rewards accordingly. Let those who witness it delight in its honors, and those who hear of it envy its fame. Thus royal culture may be purified and custom elevated. Schools were then established.
59
元帝為晉王，建武初，驃騎將軍王導上疏：
When Emperor Yuan was still Prince of Jin, at the opening of the Jianwu era, Rapid Cavalry General Wang Dao submitted a memorial:
60
:夫治化之本，在於正人倫。 人倫之正，存乎設庠序。 庠序設而五教明，則德化洽通，彝倫攸敍，有恥且格也。 父子兄弟夫婦長幼之序順，而君臣之義固矣。 易所謂正家而天下定者也。 故聖王蒙以養正，少而教之，使化沾肌骨，習以成性，有若自然，日遷善遠罪，而不自知。 行成德立，然後裁之以位。 雖王之嫡子，猶與國子齒，使知道而後貴。 其取才用士，咸先本之于學。 故周禮，鄉大夫「獻賢能之書于王，王拜而受之」。 所以尊道而貴士也。 人知士之所貴，由乎道存。 則退而修其身，修其身以及其家，正家以及於鄉，學於鄉以登於朝。 反本復始，各求諸己，敦素之業著，浮偽之道息，教使然也。 故以之事君則忠，用之莅下則仁，即孟軻所謂「未有仁而遺其親，義而後其君者也」。
The foundation of good government lies in setting human relations right. Right human relations depend on establishing schools. Once schools are in place and the Five Teachings clear, moral influence spreads, the constant relations fall into order, and people feel shame and reform themselves. The order of father and son, elder and younger brother, husband and wife, and elder and younger is restored, and the bond between ruler and minister is strengthened. This is what the Book of Changes means by "when the family is set right, the realm is settled." The sage king therefore nourished rectitude from infancy, teaching the young until moral transformation soaked into their bones, habit became nature, and day by day they drifted toward goodness and away from wrong without even knowing it. Only after conduct was formed and virtue established were they fitted to office. Even the king\'s own son was ranked alongside the other princes\' sons, taught the Way before granted eminence. In choosing talent and appointing officers, all first looked to what had been learned in school. Hence the Rites of Zhou: the district grandee "presents the roster of the worthy and able to the king, and the king bows and receives it." This is how the Way was honored and scholars valued. When people understand why scholars are honored, it is because the Way still lives among them. They withdraw to cultivate themselves; from self-cultivation they extend to family; from a well-ordered family to a well-ordered district; and from district learning they rise to serve at court. Returning to fundamentals, each searching within himself—the earnest pursuit of simplicity flourishes and shallow pretense withers. Such is the power of education. Such men serve their ruler with loyalty and govern subordinates with benevolence—precisely what Mencius meant by "there has never been a man who was benevolent yet disowned his parents, or righteous yet put his ruler last."
61
:自頃皇綱失統，禮教陵替，頌聲不興，于今二紀。 傳曰「三年不為禮，禮必壞； 三年不為樂，樂必崩」。 而況如此其久者乎？ 先進漸忘揖讓之容，後生唯聞金革之響，干戈日尋，俎豆不設，先王之道彌遠，華偽之風遂滋，非所以習民靖俗，端本抑末之謂也。 殿下以命世之資，屬當傾危之運，禮樂征伐，翼成中興，將滌穢蕩瑕，撥亂反正。 誠宜經綸稽古，建明學校，闡揚六蓺，以訓後生，使文武之道，墜而復興。 方今小雅盡廢，戎虜扇熾，節義陵遲，國恥未雪。 忠臣義士，所以扼腕拊心，禮樂政刑，當並陳以俱濟者也。 苟禮義膠固，純風載洽，則化之所陶者廣，而德之所被者大，義之所屬者深，而威之所震者遠矣。 由斯而進，則可朝服濟河，使帝典闕而復補，王綱弛而更張，饕餮改情，獸心革面，揖讓而蠻夷服，緩帶而天下從，得乎其道者，豈難也哉。 故有虞舞干戚而三苗化，魯僖作泮宮而淮夷平，桓、文之霸，皆先教而後戰。 今若聿遵前典，興復教道，使朝之子弟，並入于學，立德出身者咸習之而後通。 德路開而偽塗塞，則其化不肅而成，不嚴而治矣。 選明博修禮之士以為之師，隆教貴道，化成俗定，莫尚於斯也。
In recent years the imperial order has lost coherence, ritual teaching has fallen into ruin, and the hymns of praise have fallen silent—for two full twelve-year cycles now. The tradition says, "If ritual goes unperformed for three years, it must collapse; if music goes unperformed for three years, it must fall to ruin." And how much worse when the neglect has lasted this long? The older generation forgets the grace of bowing and yielding; the young hear only the clash of arms. War draws nearer day by day while sacrificial vessels gather dust. The way of the ancient kings recedes ever further, and the taste for ornament and pretense spreads—hardly the way to train the people, settle custom, strengthen fundamentals, and curb excess. Your Highness bears the talent of one born to reshape an age, entrusted with restoration at a moment of peril. Through ritual, music, and arms alike you have aided the revival, cleansing corruption and setting chaos aright. You should truly take counsel from antiquity, establish schools, unfold the Six Arts to instruct the young, and revive the fallen Way of civil and martial excellence. Today the Minor Odes lie abandoned; barbarian raiders burn across the land; integrity and righteousness falter; national humiliation remains unavenged. Loyal ministers and righteous men clench their fists and burn with grief. Ritual, music, governance, and punishment must be deployed together if any is to succeed. If ritual and righteousness are firmly rooted and pure influence spreads far, then transformation will reach widely, virtue will cover greatly, righteousness will run deep, and authority will be felt even at a distance. From there one might cross the Yellow River in court robes and restore what the imperial canon had lost, tighten the slackened royal net, turn savage hearts toward civilization, win the submission of barbarians through courtesy rather than force, and bind the realm with a loosened sash. Once the Way is truly grasped, would any of this be difficult? Yu danced with shield and axe and the Three Miao submitted; Duke Xi of Lu built the Pan Palace and the Huai barbarians were pacified; the hegemonies of Duke Huan and Duke Wen of Qi all rested on teaching before fighting. If we now earnestly follow the ancient canon, restore the path of education, enroll the sons of the court in schools, and require all who seek office through virtue to master their studies before advancing— then the path of virtue will open, the road of pretense will close, and transformation will succeed without severity while order is kept without harshness. Choose as teachers men of broad learning and ritual mastery; honor education and esteem the Way. Nothing surpasses this for transforming culture and fixing custom.
62
散騎常侍戴邈又上表曰：
Attendant Cavalier Dai Miao also submitted a memorial:
63
:臣聞天道之所運，莫大於陰陽； 帝王之至務，莫重於禮學。 是以古之建國，教學為先。 國有明堂辟雍之制，鄉有庠序黌校之儀，皆所以抽導幽滯，啟廣才思。 蓋以六四有困蒙之吝，君子大養正之功也。 昔仲尼列國之大夫耳，興禮修學於洙、泗之間，四方髦俊，斐然向風，受業身通者七十餘人。 自茲以來，千載寂漠，豈天下小於魯國，賢哲乏於曩時，厲與不厲故也。
I have heard that in the operation of Heaven\'s Way, nothing is greater than yin and yang; and that for emperors and kings, nothing is weightier than ritual and learning. Therefore in founding a state, education came first. The state had the Bright Hall and Royal Academy; the villages had their schools and academies—all devised to draw forth hidden talent and broaden the mind. For as the fourth line of Hexagram Six warns of a youth obstructed in learning, the superior man performs the great work of nurturing rectitude. Confucius was only a feudal grandee, yet between the Zhu and Si rivers he revived ritual and learning. Talented youths from the four quarters flocked to him, and more than seventy completed their studies and mastered the Way. Since then a thousand years have passed in silence. Is the realm smaller than Lu? Are the wise fewer than in his day? The difference lies in whether a ruler encourages learning or neglects it.
64
:自頃遭無妄之禍，社稷有綴旒之危，寇羯飲馬於長江，凶狡虎步於萬里，遂使神州蕭條，鞠為茂草，四海之內，人跡不交。 霸主有旰食之憂，黎民懷荼毒之痛，戎首交并于中原，何遽籩豆之事哉！ 然「三年不為禮，禮必壞； 三年不為樂，樂必崩」。 況曠載累紀，如此之久邪！ 今末進後生，目不覩揖讓升降之禮，耳不聞鐘鼓管弦之音，文章散滅胡馬之足，圖讖無復孑遺於世。 此蓋聖達之所深悼，有識之所咨嗟也。 夫治世尚文，遭亂尚武，文武迭用，久長之道。 譬之天地，昏明之迭，自古以來，未有不由之者也。 今或以天下未壹，非興禮學之時，此言似是而非。 夫儒道深奧，不可倉卒而成，古之俊乂，必三年而通一經，比須寇賊清夷，天下平泰，然後修之，則功成事定，誰與制禮作樂者哉！ 又貴遊之子，未必有斬將搴旗之才，亦未有從軍征戍之役，不及盛年講肄道義，使明珠加瑩磨之功，荊、隨發采琢之美，不亦良可惜乎。
Recently we have suffered undeserved calamity; the altars of state tremble like a crown about to fall. Barbarian raiders water their horses at the Yangtze; fierce enemies prowl a thousand li. The heartland lies desolate, choked with weeds; within the four seas, men scarcely meet one another. A ruler loses sleep over his meals; the people endure bitter suffering; barbarian chiefs collide at the heart of the realm—how can one speak of ritual vessels and sacrificial rites! Yet the saying runs, "If for three years no rites are performed, rites are bound to decay; if for three years no music is performed, music is bound to collapse." How much more so when generations have piled up and the lapse has lasted this long! Today the young and the newly risen have never seen the rites of bowing, yielding, ascending and descending; never heard bells, drums, strings, or pipes; belles-lettres lie trampled under barbarian hooves; and not one scrap of chart or prophecy survives in the world. This is what the sage and the clear-sighted mourn in their depths and sigh over aloud. In settled times culture is honored; in disorder arms are honored—literary and martial arts taking turns is the path to lasting rule. It is like heaven and earth, darkness and light succeeding one another—from the beginning of time, nothing has escaped this law. Some now argue that because the realm is not yet united, this is no time to revive ritual and learning—a claim that sounds plausible but is wrong. Confucian learning is deep and cannot be rushed. The finest minds of old needed three years to master a single classic. If we must wait until bandits are gone and the realm perfectly calm before we begin, then when peace is won and the work done—who will be left to frame the rites and compose the music? Moreover, sons of noble houses may never need to slay generals or haul down enemy banners, nor face conscription or frontier duty—yet they squander their prime without studying the Way and righteousness, leaving pearls unpolished and Jing and Sui jade uncut. Is that not a grievous waste?
65
:愚以世喪道久，民情玩於所習，純風日去，華競日彰，猶火之消膏而莫之覺也。 今天地造始，萬物權輿，聖朝以神武之德，值革命之運，蕩近世之流弊，繼千載之絕軌，篤道崇儒，創立大業。 明主唱之於上，宰輔篤之於下，夫上之所好，下必有過之者焉。 是故雙劍之節崇，而飛白之俗成； 挾琴之容飾，而赴曲之和作。 君子之德風，小人之德草，實在所以感之而已。 臣以闇淺，不能遠識格言，謂宜以三時之隙，漸就經始。
I hold that the world has long lost the Way; people grow slack in what they are used to; pure custom fades day by day while showy rivalry grows brighter—like fire eating away fat while no one notices. Now heaven and earth stand at a new beginning and all things are in first stir; the sacred dynasty, with divine martial virtue, meets a revolutionary age, clears away recent corruption, resumes a thousand-year broken path, holds fast to the Way and exalts Confucian learning, and lays the foundations of a great enterprise. The enlightened sovereign sings its praise above, chief ministers pursue it earnestly below—for what the ruler favors, his subjects are sure to surpass. Thus the paired-sword rite was held in honor, and the fashion of flying-white calligraphy took shape; the bearing of one who carries a qin was cultivated, and the harmony of answering song arose. The noble man\'s virtue is wind; the petty man\'s is grass—the whole matter lies in what stirs them. Your subject is dim and shallow and cannot see far; I hold that the intervals of the three farming seasons should be used to begin the work step by step.
66
太興初，議欲修立學校，唯周易王氏、尚書鄭氏、古文孔氏、毛詩周官禮記論語孝經鄭氏、春秋左傳杜氏、服氏，各置博士一人。 其儀禮公羊穀梁及鄭易，皆省不置博士。 太常荀崧上疏曰：
At the opening of the Taixing reign, officials debated establishing schools. Only for Wang\'s Changes, Zheng\'s Documents, Kong\'s ancient-text version, Mao\'s Odes, the Rites of Zhou, the Record of Rites, the Analects, the Classic of Filial Piety (Zheng\'s), the Zuo Commentary (Du\'s), and Fu\'s Spring and Autumn—one Erudite was appointed to each. The Ceremonial Rites, the Gongyang and Guliang commentaries, and Zheng\'s Changes were all cut, and no Erudites were appointed for them. Minister of Ceremonies Xun Song submitted a memorial:
67
:臣聞孔子有云，「才難，不其然乎」。 自喪亂以來，經學尤寡。 儒有席上之珍，然後能弘明道訓。 今處學則闕朝廷之秀，仕朝則廢儒學之美。 昔咸寧、太康、元康、永嘉之中，侍中、常侍、黃門之深博道奧，通洽古今，行為世表者，領國子博士。 一則應對殿堂，奉酬顧問； 二則參訓門子，以弘儒學； 三則祠、儀二曹，及太常之職，以得藉用質疑。 今皇朝中興，美隆往初，宜憲章令軌，祖述前典。
I have heard Confucius say, "Talent is hard to find—is this not so?" Since the age of ruin and disorder, classical learning has grown especially thin. Only when a Confucian scholar holds treasures fit for the mat can he broadly illuminate the teachings of the Way. Today if one remains in study the court lacks its finest minds; if one enters office the beauty of Confucian learning is cast aside. In the Xianking, Taikang, Yuankang, and Yongjia reigns, Palace Attendants, Regular Attendants, and Yellow Gate officials who were deeply versed in the Way, thoroughly learned in past and present, and whose conduct was a model for the age served as Directors of Erudites of the Imperial University. First, they answered in the hall and court, responding to the sovereign\'s questions; second, they helped instruct the sons of nobles and spread Confucian learning; third, in the bureaus of Sacrificial Affairs and Ceremonial Protocol and in the office of Minister of Ceremonies, they could be drawn on to resolve doubts. Now the dynasty has revived in splendor surpassing its first founding; the present statutes should be taken as law and the former canon followed.
68
:世祖武皇帝聖德欽明，應運登禪，受終于魏。 崇儒興學，治致升平。 經始明堂，營建辟雍，告朔班政，鄉飲大射，西閤東序，圖書禁籍，臺省有宗廟太府金墉故事，太學有石經古文。 先儒典訓，賈、馬、鄭、杜、服、孔、王、何、顏、尹之徒，章句傳注眾家之學，置博士十九人。 九州之中，師徒相傳，學士如林，猶是選張華、劉寔居太常之官，以重儒教。
Emperor Wu, Founding Ancestor, possessed sacred virtue and reverent wisdom; he answered Heaven\'s call, ascended by abdication, and received the throne from Wei. He exalted Confucian learning and revived the schools, governing until peace and plenty were achieved. He began the Bright Hall, built the Imperial Academy, announced the new moon and promulgated policy, held district feasts and archery rites; the Western Pavilion and Eastern Gallery held books and restricted texts; the ministries kept records of the ancestral temples, the Grand Treasury, and the Jin Fort; and the Imperial University held stone classics in ancient script. For the canonical teachings of earlier Confucians—Jia, Ma, Zheng, Du, Fu, Kong, Wang, He, Yan, Yin, and others—and the many schools of commentary and gloss, nineteen Erudites were appointed. Across the Nine Provinces masters and disciples handed learning down and scholars stood thick as a forest—yet even then Zhang Hua and Liu Shi were chosen as Ministers of Ceremonies to give weight to Confucian teaching.
69
:傳稱「孔子沒而微言絕，七十子終而大義乖」。 自頃中夏殄瘁，講誦遏密，斯文之道，將墜于地。 陛下聖哲龍飛，闡弘祖烈，申命儒術，恢崇道教，樂正雅、頌，於是乎在。 江、揚二州，先漸聲教，學士遺文，於今為盛； 然方之疇昔，猶千之一也。 臣學不章句，才不弘道，階緣光寵，遂忝非服，方之華、寔，儒風邈遠，思竭駑駘，庶增萬分，願斯道隆於百代之上，搢紳詠於千載之下。
Tradition says, "When Confucius died, subtle words ceased; when the seventy disciples passed away, the great meaning was lost." Recently the Central Plain has been laid waste; lectures and recitation have been stifled; this culture is about to fall to the ground. Your Majesty, sage and wise, arose like a dragon; you expanded the achievements of your ancestors, renewed the mandate of Confucian learning, restored and exalted the teaching of the Way—and the music directors for the Ya and Song are here once more. In Jiang and Yang, civilizing influence came first; scholars and surviving writings are today at their fullest; yet compared with former times, this is still only one part in a thousand. Your subject\'s learning does not reach to commentarial glosses; my talent cannot broadly proclaim the Way. Step by step I have climbed by grace to rank I do not deserve. Beside Hua and Shi, the Confucian wind is far away. I would exhaust my feeble strength, hoping to add one ten-thousandth—and pray that this Way may rise above a hundred generations and that gentry may sing its praise a thousand years hence.
70
:伏聞節省之制，皆三分置二，博士舊員十有九人，今五經合九人。 準古計今，猶未中半。 九人以外，猶宜增四。 願陛下萬機餘暇，時垂省覽。 周易一經，有鄭玄注，其書根源，誠可深惜，宜為鄭易博士一人。 儀禮一經，所謂曲禮，鄭玄於禮特明，皆有證據，宜置鄭儀禮博士一人。 春秋公羊，其書精隱，明於斷獄，宜置博士一人。 穀梁簡約隱要，宜存於世，置博士一人。 昔周之衰，下陵上替，臣弒其君，子弒其父，上無天子，下無方伯，善者誰賞，惡者誰罰，綱紀亂矣。 孔子懼而作春秋，諸侯諱妬，懼犯時禁，是以微辭妙旨，義不顯明，故曰「知我者其唯春秋，罪我者其唯春秋」。 時左丘明、子夏造膝親受，無不精究。 孔子既沒，微言將絕，於是丘明退撰所聞而為之傳。 其書善禮，多膏腴美辭，張本繼末，以發明經意，信多奇偉，學者好之。 儒者稱公羊高親受子夏，立於漢朝，辭義清俊，斷決明審，多可採用，董仲舒之所善也。 穀梁赤師徒相傳，暫立於漢，時劉向父子，漢之名儒、猶執一家，莫肯相從。 其書文清義約，諸所發明，或是左氏、公羊所不載，亦足有所訂正，是以三傳並行於先代，通才未能孤廢。 今去聖久遠，斯文將墜，與其過廢，寧過而立也。 臣以為三傳雖同一春秋，而發端異趣。 案如三家異同之說，此乃義則戰爭之場，辭亦劍戟之鋒，於理不可得共。 博士宜各置一人，以傳其學。
I have heard that austerity keeps only two of every three posts; the old establishment of Erudites numbered nineteen, but now the Five Classics together have nine. Measured against antiquity and weighed against the present, this is still not even half. Beyond these nine, four more should still be added. I pray that Your Majesty, in the leisure left from the myriad affairs of state, will from time to time look into this. The Changes alone has Zheng Xuan\'s commentary; the roots of that work would be a deep loss—it is fitting to appoint one Erudite for Zheng\'s Changes. The Ceremonial Rites, known as the Detailed Rites—Zheng Xuan was especially clear on ritual, with evidence throughout; one Erudite for Zheng\'s Ceremonial Rites should be appointed. The Gongyang Commentary on the Spring and Autumn is refined and recondite, clear on judging legal cases; one Erudite should be appointed. The Guliang is concise and holds hidden essentials; it should be preserved in the world—appoint one Erudite. In ancient times when Zhou declined, the lower overran the higher; ministers murdered their lords and sons murdered their fathers; above there was no Son of Heaven, below no regional lords; who rewarded the good, who punished the evil? The bonds of law and decorum fell into chaos. Confucius in fear compiled the Spring and Autumn. The feudal lords were jealous and guarded their names, fearing to violate the prohibitions of the age—so he used subtle words and refined meaning, never stating his purpose openly; hence he said, "Those who understand me—it can only be through the Spring and Autumn; those who condemn me—it can only be through the Spring and Autumn." At that time Zuo Qiuming and Zixia sat close enough to touch his knee and received instruction directly—nothing was left unexamined. After Confucius died, subtle words were about to cease; then Qiuming withdrew and compiled what he had heard into a commentary. That book excels in ritual, abounds in rich and beautiful language, sets forth origins and carries conclusions forward to elucidate the classic—truly full of marvels and grandeur; scholars have loved it. Confucian scholars say Gongyang Gao received instruction directly from Zixia; it was established in the Han dynasty; its language and meaning are clear and refined, its judgments bright and precise—much can be adopted; this is what Dong Zhongshu favored. Guliang Chi passed it down from master to disciple; it was briefly established in Han. At that time Liu Xiang and his son, famous Confucians of Han, each clung to one school and would not follow the other. That book\'s text is clear and its meaning concise; various elucidations—some not recorded in the Zuo or Gongyang traditions—are also enough to correct errors; hence the Three Commentaries circulated side by side in earlier ages, and men of comprehensive talent could not simply discard any one alone. Now we are far from the Sage; this culture is about to fall—better to err on the side of establishing than on the side of abolishing. Your subject holds that although the Three Commentaries all treat the same Spring and Autumn, they begin from different aims. Examining the divergent and convergent doctrines of the three schools—this is a battlefield of meaning, and in language also the edge of sword and spear—in principle they cannot be combined. Erudites should be appointed one apiece to transmit each tradition.
71
元帝詔曰：「崧表如此，皆經國大務，而為治所由。 息馬投戈，猶可講藝。 今雖日不暇給，豈忘本而遺存邪。 可共博議之。 」有司奏宜如崧表。 詔曰：「穀梁膚淺，不足立博士。 餘如所奏。 」會王敦之難，事不施行。
Emperor Yuan\'s edict said: "Xun Song\'s memorial is as stated—these are all great affairs of governing the state and the foundations from which good order arises. Even when horses are rested and weapons cast aside, one may still lecture on the arts. Though today the days leave no surplus, would we forget the root and abandon what must endure? Let this be broadly debated together." The relevant offices memorialized that it should be as Xun Song proposed. An edict said: "The Guliang is superficial—insufficient to establish an Erudite. The rest as memorialized." Just then came Wang Dun\'s rebellion; the matter was not carried out.
72
成帝咸康三年，國子祭酒袁瓌、太常馮懷又上疏曰：
In the third year of Xiankang under Emperor Cheng, Director of the Imperial University Yuan Huan and Minister of Ceremonies Feng Huai again submitted a memorial:
73
:臣聞先王之教也，崇典訓，明禮學，以示後生，道萬物之性，暢為善之道也。 宗周既興，文史載煥，端委治於南蠻，頌聲逸於四海。 故延州入聘，聞雅音而嗟咨，韓起適魯，觀易象而歎息。 何者？ 立人之道，於此為首也。 孔子恂恂，道化洙、泗，孟軻皇皇，誨誘無倦。 是以仁義之聲，于今猶存，禮讓之風，千載未泯。
I have heard that in the teaching of former kings, canonical instruction was exalted and ritual learning made clear, to show later generations the nature of the ten thousand things and unfold the way of goodness. When the Zhou house arose, its culture and records blazed forth; clothed in formal robes it governed the southern barbarians, and songs of praise spread beyond the four seas. Hence when Yanzhou came on a diplomatic mission and heard the elegant tones, he sighed in admiration; when Han Qi went to Lu and observed the Images of the Changes, he breathed deep in wonder. Why was this so? Because the foundation of establishing humanity lies here above all. Confucius was gentle and earnest, transforming the lands of Zhu and Si with the Way; Mencius went forth urgently, teaching and guiding without weariness. Thus the voice of benevolence and righteousness survives even today; the wind of ritual and yielding has not perished in a thousand years.
74
:疇昔陵替，喪亂屢臻，儒林之教暫頹，庠序之禮有闕，國學索然，墳卷莫啟，有心之徒，抱志無由。 昔魏武身親介冑，務在武功，猶尚息鞍披覽，投戈吟詠，以為世之所須者，治之本宜崇。 況今陛下以聖明臨朝，百官以虔恭莅事，朝野無虞，江外靜謐。 如之何泱泱之風，漠焉無聞，洋洋之美，墜於聖世乎。 古人有言，詩書義之府，禮樂德之則。 實宜留心經籍，闡明學義，使諷頌之音，盈於京室，味道之賢，是則是詠，豈不盛哉！
In former times order collapsed and calamity came again and again; instruction in the forest of scholars temporarily declined; the rites of the village schools were neglected; the state academy stood desolate, the tomb-texts lay unopened; those with resolve embraced their purpose but found no path forward. In olden days Cao Cao personally donned armor and helmet, devoted to martial achievement—yet he still favored resting his saddle to read, casting aside weapons to recite poetry, holding that what the age required—the foundation of governance—ought to be exalted. How much more so now, when Your Majesty presides over court in sage illumination, the hundred officials perform their duties in reverent devotion, court and countryside are untroubled, and beyond the Yangtze all is tranquil. How can it be that the vast and surging wind of culture is heard no more in silence, and the grand and abundant beauty falls away in a sage age? The ancients said: the Odes and Documents are the treasury of righteousness; ritual and music are the standard of virtue. One truly ought to attend to the classics, elucidate the meaning of learning, so that the tones of recitation and praise fill the capital, and worthy men who have tasted the flavor of the Way take them as models and sing their praise—would this not be magnificent!
75
疏奏，帝有感焉。 由是議立國學，徵集生徒，而世尚莊、老，莫肯用心儒訓。 穆帝永和八年，殷浩西征，以軍興罷遣，由此遂廢。
The memorial was submitted; the Emperor was moved. From this there was discussion of establishing the state academy and gathering students—but the age favored Zhuangzi and Laozi, and none would apply themselves to Confucian instruction. In the eighth year of Yonghe under Emperor Mu, Yin Hao marched west on campaign; the academy was dismissed for military mobilization, and from this it was abandoned.
76
征西將軍庾亮在武昌，開置學官。 教曰：
The General Who Conquers the West, Yu Liang, at Wuchang, opened and established school officials. His instruction read:
77
:人情重交而輕財，好逸而惡勞，學業致苦，而祿答未厚，由捷徑者多，故莫肯用心。 洙、泗邈遠，風、雅彌替，後生放任，不復憲章典謨。 臨官宰政者，務目前之治，不能閑以典誥。 遂令詩、書荒塵，頌聲寂漠，仰瞻俯省，能弗歎慨。 自胡夷交侵，殆三十年矣。 而未革面嚮風者，豈威武之用盡，抑文教未洽，不足綏之邪？ 昔魯秉周禮，齊不敢侮； 范會崇典，晉國以治。 楚、魏之君，皆阻帶山河，憑城據漢，國富民殷，而不能保其強大，吳起、屈完所以為歎也。 由此言之，禮義之固，孰與金城湯池？ 季路稱攝乎大國之間，加之以師旅，因之以饑饉，為之三年，猶欲行其義方。 況今江表晏然，王道隆盛，而不能弘敷禮樂，敦明庠序，其何以訓彝倫而來遠人乎！ 魏武帝於馳騖之時，以馬上為家，逮于建安之末，風塵未弭，然猶留心遠覽，大學興業，所謂顛沛必於是，真通才也。
Human nature esteems connections and undervalues wealth, loves ease and hates labor; study brings hardship, yet salary and reward are not ample; because shortcuts are many, none apply themselves with care. The Zhu and Si rivers are far away; the Feng and Ya odes fade ever more; the later generation grows unrestrained, no longer patterning themselves on the canonical edicts. Those who hold office and govern affairs pursue only present-day administration; they cannot spare leisure for the classic commands. The Odes and Documents are thus left to dust and desolation, songs of praise fall silent—and looking up and looking within, who could fail to sigh? Since the barbarians of Hu and Yi have pressed in together, it has been nearly thirty years. Yet those who have not changed their faces and turned toward our wind—is it that martial might has been exhausted, or that civil teaching has not reached them, insufficient to win them over? In olden days Lu upheld the Zhou rituals—and Qi did not dare insult it; Fan Hui exalted the canon—and Jin was thereby governed. The rulers of Chu and Wei, each shielded by mountains and rivers, relying on strong walls and holding the Han—their states were rich and their people prosperous, yet they could not preserve their strength; this is why Wu Qi and Qu Wan lamented. From this it may be said: what fortified wall or boiling moat compares with the strength of ritual and righteousness? Zilu once said that even dwelling among great states, with army campaigns added and famine following, and dwelling so for three years—he would still wish to practice the method of righteousness. How much more so today, when the lands south of the Yangtze are tranquil and the royal Way flourishes—yet we cannot broadly spread ritual and music or earnestly illuminate the village schools—by what means shall we instruct the constant norms and draw distant peoples near! Cao Cao, even in the midst of galloping campaigns, made his home in the saddle; by the end of the Jian\'an era, though the dust of war had not settled, he still attended to far-reaching study and revived the Great Learning—what is called finding necessity precisely in adversity; truly a man of comprehensive talent.
78
:今使三時既務，五教並修，軍旅已整，俎豆無廢，豈非兼善者哉！ 便處分安學校處所，籌量起立講舍。 參佐大將子弟，悉令入學，吾家子弟，亦令受業。 四府博學識義通涉文學經綸者，建儒林祭酒，使班同三署，厚其供給，皆妙選邦彥，必有其宜者，以充此舉。 近臨川、臨賀二郡，並求修復學校，可下聽之。 若非束脩之流，禮教所不及，而欲階緣免役者，不得為生。 明為條制，令法清而人貴。
With the three seasons' work already in hand, the five teachings pursued together, the armies already in order, and the ritual vessels never neglected—is this not true excellence in both war and peace! He immediately set aside sites for schools and planned where to build lecture halls. The sons and younger kinsmen of staff officers and generals were all sent to school, and the younger men of his own household were ordered to study as well. From the four ministries he chose men of broad learning, moral discernment, and literary and political skill to establish a Libationer of the Confucian Forest, with rank equal to the Three Offices and generous support. Only the finest scholars of the realm were to be selected; surely suitable men could be found for the post. Recently both Linchuan and Linhe commanderies had asked to repair their schools; the request was approved and sent down. Anyone outside the proper student body, beyond the reach of ritual instruction, who sought connections to escape labor service was not to be enrolled. Regulations were set out plainly so that the law would be clear and learning would be honored.
79
又繕造禮器俎豆之屬，將行大射之禮。 亮尋薨，又廢。
Ritual vessels—stands, cups, and the like—were also made ready for the great archery ceremony. Liang soon died, and the project was abandoned once more.
80
孝武帝太元九年，尚書謝石又陳之曰：
In the ninth year of Emperor Xiaowu's Taixuan reign, Master of Writing Xie Shi submitted another memorial:
81
:立人之道，曰仁與義。 翼善輔性，唯禮與學。 雖理出自然，必須誘導。 故洙、泗闡弘道之風，詩、書垂軌教之典。 敦詩悅禮，王化以斯而隆； 甄陶九流，羣生於是乎穆。 世不常治，道亦時亡。 光武投戈而習誦，魏武息馬以修學，懼墜斯文，若此之至也。 大晉受命，值世多阻，雖聖化日融，而王道未備，庠序之業，或廢或興。 遂令陶鑄闕日用之功，民性靡素絲之益，亹亹玄緒，翳焉莫抽，臣所以遠尋伏念，寤寐永歎者也。
The way to establish a human being is through benevolence and righteousness. To foster goodness and shape character, nothing serves better than ritual and learning. Though principle is innate, it must still be cultivated and guided. That is why the stream of the Way flowed from Zhu and Si, and why the Odes and Documents handed down the canonical models of instruction. Revering the Odes and delighting in ritual, royal transformation rose accordingly; and by refining every current of learning, the people were brought to harmony. The world is not always well governed, and the Way too is lost from time to time. Emperor Guangwu laid down his weapons to study the classics; Cao Cao halted his campaigns to promote learning—such was their dread of letting civilization collapse. When Great Jin received the Mandate, the age was full of obstacles. Though sagely influence spread day by day, the royal Way was still incomplete, and the work of the schools was now abandoned, now revived. The daily work of moral shaping was left undone; the people gained none of the refining benefit of raw silk; the subtle thread of learning lay buried and could not be drawn out. That is why your servant, searching far in humble thought, sighs without rest, waking or sleeping.
82
:今皇威遐震，戎車方靜，將灑玄風於四區，導斯民於至德。 豈可不弘敷禮樂，使煥乎可觀。 請興復國學，以訓冑子； 班下州郡，普修鄉校。 雕琢琳琅，和寶必至，大啟羣蒙，茂茲成德。 匪懈于事，必由之以通，則人競其業，道隆學備矣。
Now imperial majesty reaches the far corners, and the chariots of war have just stilled. It is time to spread the subtle wind across the realm and lead the people to supreme virtue. How can ritual and music not be broadly restored, so that they shine forth for all to see? I beg that the National University be revived to instruct the sons of the nobility; and that orders be sent to the provinces and commanderies to restore local schools everywhere. Polish jade and gems, and matching treasures will come of themselves; open wide the untaught masses, and cultivated virtue will flourish. If the work is pursued without slackening and carried through to completion, people will vie in their studies, the Way will rise high, and learning will be whole.
83
烈宗納其言。 其年，選公卿二千石子弟為生，增造廟屋一百五十五間。 而品課無章，士君子恥與其列。 國子祭酒殷茂言之曰：
Emperor Xiaowu accepted his proposal. That year sons of high ministers and two-thousand-shi officials were chosen as students, and one hundred fifty-five new academy halls were built. Yet rank and evaluation had no clear standards, and gentlemen were ashamed to be counted among the students. Yin Mao, Libationer of the National University, addressed the matter:
84
:臣聞弘化正俗，存乎禮教，輔性成德，必資於學。 先王所以陶鑄天下，津梁萬物，閑邪納善，潛被於日用者也。 故能疏通玄理，窮綜幽微，一貫古今，彌綸治化。 且夫子稱回，以好學為本，七十希仰，以善誘歸宗。 雅、頌之音，流詠千載，聖賢之淵範，哲王所同風。
Your servant has heard that to spread transformation and set custom right one must rely on ritual instruction, and that character and virtue are completed only through learning. By this the former kings molded the realm, bridged all things, turned aside evil and received goodness, quietly suffusing daily life. Thus they could open subtle principle, exhaust the hidden and minute, thread past and present together, and weave governance and transformation into one whole. The Master praised Hui for loving learning above all else; at seventy, few could match him, for through skillful guidance one returns to the root. The tones of the Ya and Song have flowed in song for a thousand years—the deep model of sages and worthies, the common wind of wise kings.
85
:自大晉中興，肇基江左，崇明學校，修建庠序，公卿子弟，並入國學。 尋值多故，訓業不終。 陛下以聖德玄一，思隆前美，順通居方，導達物性，興復儒肆，僉與後生。 自學建彌年，而功無可名。 憚業避役，就存者無幾，或假託親疾，真偽難知，聲實渾亂，莫此之甚。 臣聞舊制，國子生皆冠族華冑，比列皇儲。 而中者混雜蘭艾，遂令人情恥之。 子貢去朔之餼羊，仲尼猶愛其禮，況名實兼喪，面牆一世者乎。 若以當今急病，未遑斯典，權宜停廢者，別一理也。 若其不然，宜依舊準。 竊謂羣臣內外，清官子姪，普應入學，制以程課。 今者見生，或年在扞格，方圓殊趣，宜聽其去就，各從所安。 所上謬合，乞付外參議。
Since the restoration of Jin south of the Yangtze, schools were honored, academies built and repaired, and sons of high ministers all entered the National University. Soon troubles multiplied, and instruction was never carried through. Your Majesty, with unified sagely virtue, seeks to raise up former excellence, harmonizing with the directions and guiding the nature of things, and has revived the halls of Confucian learning so that all may join the younger generation. Years have passed since the schools were founded, yet there is nothing to show for it. Students shun their work and dodge service; few actually remain. Some falsely plead parental illness, and truth and pretense are hard to tell apart. Name and reality are utterly confused—nothing is worse. Your servant has heard that under the old system National University students were all from eminent clans and noble houses, ranked alongside the imperial heir's sons. Now orchid and mugwort are mixed together, and public sentiment is ashamed of the institution. When Zigong wished to abolish the lamb offered at the new moon, Confucius still upheld the ritual—how much more when name and reality are both lost and one remains ignorant for a lifetime! If today's urgent troubles leave no room for this institution and it is provisionally suspended, that is another matter. If not, the old standard should be followed. Your servant privately holds that sons and nephews of officials within and without the court, from respectable official families, should all enter school under a fixed curriculum and examination system. As for current students, some are at a stubborn age and differ widely in temperament; they should be allowed to stay or leave, each as he chooses. What I have submitted may be mistaken; I beg that it be referred for external deliberation.
86
烈宗下詔褒納，又不施行。 朝廷及草萊之人有志於學者，莫不發憤歎息。
Emperor Xiaowu issued an edict praising and accepting the proposal, yet once again nothing was done. Throughout the court and among commoners who cared for learning, none failed to burn with indignation and sigh.
87
清河人李遼又上表曰：「臣聞教者，治化之本，人倫之始，所以誘達羣方，進德興仁，譬諸土石，陶冶成器。 雖復百王殊禮，質文參差，至於斯道，其用不爽。 自中華湮沒，闕里荒毀，先王之澤寢，聖賢之風絕，自此迄今，將及百年。 造化有靈，否終以泰，河、濟夷徙，海、岱清通，黎庶蒙蘇，鳬藻奮化。 而典訓弗敷，雅、頌寂蔑，久凋之俗，大弊未改。 非演迪斯文，緝熙宏猷，將何以光贊時邕，克隆盛化哉。 事有如賒而急，實此之謂也。 亡父先臣回，綏集邦邑，歸誠本朝。 以太元十年，遣臣奉表。 路經闕里，過覲孔廟，庭宇傾頓，軌式頹弛，萬世宗匠，忽焉淪廢，仰瞻俯慨，不覺涕流。 既達京輦，表求興復聖祀，修建講學。 至十四年十一月十七日，奉被明詔，采臣鄙議，敕下兗州魯郡，準舊營飾。 故尚書令謝石令臣所須列上，又出家布，薄助興立。 故鎮北將軍譙王恬版臣行北魯縣令，賜許供遣。 二臣薨徂，成規不遂。 陛下體唐堯文思之美，訪宣尼善誘之勤，矜荒餘之凋昧，愍聲教之未浹。 愚謂可重符兗州刺史，遂成舊廟，蠲復數戶，以供掃灑。 并賜給六經，講立庠序，延請宿學，廣集後進，使油然入道，發剖琢之功。 運仁義以征伐，敷道德以服遠，何招而不懷，何柔而不從。 所為者微，所弘甚大。 臣自致身輦轂，于今八稔，違親轉積，夙夜匪寧。 振武將軍何澹之今震扞三齊，臣當隨反。 裴回天邑，感戀罔極。 乞臣表付外參議。 」又不見省。 宋高祖受命，詔有司立學，未就而崩。 太祖元嘉二十年，復立國子學，二十七年廢。
Li Liao of Qinghe submitted another memorial: "Your servant has heard that teaching is the root of governance and the beginning of human relations—the means by which the many are guided, virtue advanced, and benevolence raised, like clay and stone shaped in the kiln into useful vessels. Though the hundred kings differed in ritual and substance and ornament varied, the use of this Way never failed. Since the heartland fell, Queli lay in ruins, the grace of the former kings faded, and the wind of sages and worthies was cut off—from then until now nearly a hundred years have passed. Creation has its spirit: after long decline comes renewal. The Yellow and Ji rivers run clear, the sea and Mount Tai stand open, the people revive, and the realm stirs with new life. Yet canonical instruction is not spread abroad; the Ya and Song lie silent; the deep corruption of long decay is not yet set right. Unless this culture is spread and these great designs gathered into light, how can the age be harmonized and flourishing transformation multiplied? Some matters seem remote yet are urgent—this is one of them. My late father, the former subject Hui, pacified the commandery, gathered the people, and pledged loyalty to this court. In the tenth year of Taixuan he sent me to submit a memorial. On the road I passed through Queli and visited the Temple of Confucius. The buildings had collapsed, the rites fallen into decay—the master craftsman of ten thousand generations lay suddenly in ruin. Gazing up and down, I wept without knowing it. On reaching the capital I submitted a memorial asking that sacrifice to the Sage be revived and lectures and learning restored. On the seventeenth day of the eleventh month of the fourteenth year I received an imperial edict adopting my humble proposal and ordering Yan Province and Lu Commandery to restore the buildings according to the old standard. The late Director of the Masters of Writing Xie Shi listed and submitted the supplies I required and also contributed household cloth as a modest contribution to the work. The late General Who Pacifies the North, Prince Qiao of Qiao, appointed me acting magistrate of North Lu County and authorized supplies and transport. Both ministers died, and the plan was never completed. Your Majesty embodies the literary thought of Emperor Yao, seeks the diligent guidance of Confucius, pities the decay of what survives in ruins, and grieves that instruction has not yet reached every corner of the realm. I humbly propose that the Inspector of Yan Province again be ordered by imperial rescript to complete the old temple, exempt several households, and assign them to its upkeep. Grant the Six Classics, establish schools and lectures, invite veteran scholars, gather young students in numbers, and let them enter the Way as naturally as oil spreads—unleashing the work of cutting and polishing. Wield benevolence and righteousness in war, spread virtue to win the distant—who would not come when called, who would not submit when treated with kindness? The deed itself is small; what it spreads is vast. I myself have served at the capital for eight years now; separation from my parents has grown long, and day and night I have known no peace. General Who Strengthens the Military He Tanzhi now pacifies the three Qi regions, and I should return with him. As I turn back toward the capital, my gratitude and longing know no bounds. I beg that my memorial be referred for external deliberation. Again it was not examined. When the Founding Emperor of Song received the Mandate, he ordered the relevant offices to establish schools, but died before the work was finished. In the twentieth year of Emperor Wen's Yuanjia reign the National University was restored; in the twenty-seventh year it was abolished.

魏高貴鄉公甘露三年，車駕親率羣司行養老之禮於太學。 於是王祥為三老，鄭小同為五更。 今無其注，然漢禮具存也。
In the third year of Ganlu, under the Noble Township Lord of Wei, the emperor personally led the assembled officials in performing the rite of nourishing the aged at the Imperial Academy. Wang Xiang served as Elder of the Three, and Zheng Xiaotong as Fifth Watch. No commentary on this survives today, yet the Han rites remain fully recorded.

晉武帝泰始六年十二月，帝臨辟雍，行鄉飲酒之禮。 詔曰：「禮儀之廢久矣，乃今復講肄舊典。 賜太常絹百匹，丞、博士及學生牛酒。 」咸寧三年，惠帝元康九年，復行其禮。
In the twelfth month of the sixth year of Jin Emperor Wu's Taishi reign, the emperor visited the Imperial Academy and performed the district drinking ceremony. The edict read: "Ritual and ceremony have long lain in ruin; only now are the old canons again studied and practiced. Grant the Director of Ceremonies one hundred bolts of silk, and oxen and wine to the vice director, academicians, and students. In the third year of Xianning and the ninth year of Emperor Hui's Yuankang reign, the rite was performed again.

魏齊王正始中，齊王每講經遍，輒使太常釋奠先聖先師於辟雍，弗躬親。 晉惠帝、明帝之為太子，及愍懷太子講經竟，並親釋奠於太學，太子進爵於先師，中庶子進爵於顏淵。 元帝詔曰：「吾識太子此事，祠訖便請王公以下者，昔在洛時，嘗豫清坐也。 」成、穆、孝武三帝，亦皆親釋奠。 孝武時，以太學在水南懸遠，有司議依升平元年，於中堂權立行太學。 于時無復國子生，有司奏：「應須二學生百二十人。 太學生取見人六十，國子生權銓大臣子孫六十人，事訖罷。 」奏可。 釋奠禮畢，會百官六品以上。 元嘉二十二年，太子釋奠，采晉故事，官有其注。 祭畢，太祖親臨學宴會，太子以下悉豫。
In the Zhengshi era under the Qi King of Wei, whenever the king finished lecturing on the classics, he had the Director of Ceremonies perform the libation to the former sages and former masters at the Imperial Academy—he did not attend in person. When Emperors Hui and Ming were crown princes, and when Crown Prince Minhuai finished lecturing on the classics, each personally performed the libation at the Imperial Academy: the crown prince advanced in rank before the former master, and the Palace Companion before Yan Yuan. Emperor Yuan's edict said: "I remember when the crown prince did this—after the sacrifice he would invite the princes and dukes and those below; in Luoyang we once sat together in quiet audience. Emperors Cheng, Mu, and Xiaowu likewise all performed the libation in person. In Emperor Xiaowu's time, because the Imperial Academy south of the river was remote, the relevant offices proposed, following the first year of Shengping, to establish a provisional Imperial Academy in the central hall. At the time there were no longer National University students; the relevant offices memorialized: "One hundred twenty students from the two schools will be required. Take sixty Imperial Academy students from those presently enrolled, and provisionally select sixty National University students from the sons and grandsons of great ministers; when the affair is finished, dismiss them. The memorial was approved. When the libation rite was finished, officials of the sixth rank and above were assembled. In the twenty-second year of Yuanjia the crown prince performed the libation, following the Jin precedent; the offices had their commentary on the rite. When the sacrifice was finished, Emperor Wen personally attended the academy banquet; the crown prince and all below were present.
